100806.q: Which ancient people already chewed the sap of a tree as chewing gum?
100806.e: The Maya in Central America chewed the thickened sap of the sapodilla tree. This substance is called chicle.
100806.m: The Maya were already chewing gum.

100807.e: Chewing gum sticks to the ground and is very hard to remove. Cleaning it up costs municipalities a lot of money.
100807.m: Chewing gum belongs in the bin.

100808.q: Why can sugar-free chewing gum help your teeth after eating?
a: It increases the flow of saliva
It makes your teeth as white as snow
It fills holes in your teeth
100808.e: When you chew, your mouth makes more saliva. Saliva helps to dilute acids in the mouth. But it doesn't replace brushing your teeth.

100809.q: Which country has largely banned the sale of chewing gum?
100809.e: In Singapore the sale of chewing gum has been largely banned since 1992. This is to keep streets and trains clean.
100809.m: Chewing gum is largely banned in Singapore.

100810.q: What is the gum base of most chewing gum made of today?
100810.e: In the past chewing gum was made from tree sap. Today the gum base is usually made artificially from plastic-like substances.
100810.m: Today's chewing gum is mostly made artificially.

100811.q: Which part of an earthworm that has been cut in two can sometimes survive?
a: The front part with the head
100811.e: Only the front part can survive, if enough of the body is left. The back part usually dies.
100811.m: Only the front part of an earthworm can survive.

100812.q: An earthworm loses a small piece of its back end. What often happens?
a: The piece becomes a new worm
It immediately gets shorter and fatter
100812.e: If an earthworm loses a piece of its back end, it can often grow back. But a whole new worm doesn't grow from it.
100812.m: An earthworm can replace its back end.

100813.q: How many pairs of “hearts” does an earthworm have?
100813.e: The earthworm has five pairs of heart arches. They pump its blood around the body.
100813.m: The earthworm has five pairs of hearts.

100814.q: What is an earthworm's body made of?
100814.e: An earthworm's body is made of lots of rings, called segments. The common earthworm has over a hundred.
100814.m: An earthworm is made of lots of rings.

100815.q: How long can the common earthworm grow?
100815.e: The common earthworm is usually 9 to 30 centimetres long. In the tropics there are much longer species.
100815.m: An earthworm grows up to about 30 centimetres long.

100817.q: When do you often see earthworms on paths and roads?
100817.e: When it rains, the ground is wet. Then lots of earthworms crawl to the surface and onto the paths.
100817.m: Earthworms come out when it rains.

100818.q: Do you get warts if you touch a toad?
a: Yes, but only on your feet
100818.e: You don't get warts from toads. That is an old superstition.

100819.e: Warts are caused by viruses. You can catch them in swimming pools, for example.

100820.q: What are the bumps on the skin of a common toad good for?
100820.e: The bumps release a substance that tastes nasty. So enemies often leave the toad alone.
100820.m: A toad's bumps put off enemies.

100821.q: Why are small fences put up along roads in spring?
100821.e: In spring toads migrate to their ponds. The fences stop them so that helpers can carry them safely across the road.
100821.m: Toad fences save toads from the traffic.

100822.q: Which animal group do toads belong to?
100822.e: Toads are amphibians, like frogs and newts. They live on land and in water.

100823.q: What is a toad's skin usually like compared with a frog's?
100823.e: Frogs usually have smooth, moist skin. Toads, on the other hand, tend to have dry skin with lots of bumps.

100824.q: Which animals does a common toad like to eat?
100824.e: Common toads hunt slugs, snails, worms and insects at night. That is why they are useful in the garden.
100824.m: Toads eat slugs, snails and insects.

100825.q: Can you see the Great Wall of China from space with the naked eye?
a: Yes, very easily at any time
100825.e: The wall is very long, but only a few metres wide. From space you can hardly see it with the naked eye, or not at all.
100825.m: You can't see the Great Wall of China from space.

100826.q: What did the first Chinese astronaut report about the wall?
a: He saw it from the Moon
100826.e: In 2003 Yang Liwei became the first Chinese person to fly into space. Afterwards he said he had not seen the wall.
100826.m: Even a Chinese astronaut didn't see the wall.

100827.q: Why is the wall so hard to make out from space?
a: It is narrow and the same colour as its surroundings
100827.e: The wall is narrow and built from stone and earth. That is why it hardly stands out from the landscape.
100827.m: The wall blends into the landscape.

100828.q: Roughly how long is the Great Wall of China with all its sections?
100828.e: A survey in 2012 found that all the sections together come to over 21,000 kilometres. It is the longest structure in the world.
100828.m: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure in the world.

100829.q: Why was the Great Wall of China built?
100829.e: The wall was meant to protect China from horse-riding peoples from the north. It was built over many centuries.
100829.m: The wall was meant to protect China.

100830.q: What was the Great Wall of China built from?
100830.e: Depending on the area, the workers built with stone, bricks or rammed earth. They used whatever was available locally.
100830.m: The wall is made of stone, bricks and earth.

100831.q: Which list has the Great Wall of China been on since 1987?
100831.e: Since 1987 the Great Wall of China has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is seen as an important heritage of humanity.
100831.m: The Great Wall of China is a World Heritage Site.

100832.q: Near which capital city is it easy to visit the Great Wall of China?
100832.e: Well-known sections such as Badaling lie north of Beijing. Huge numbers of people visit the wall there.
100832.m: You can visit the wall near Beijing.

100833.q: What were the towers on the Great Wall of China for?
100833.e: Guards kept watch from the towers. They passed on signals using smoke and fire.
100833.m: The towers on the wall were watchtowers.

100834.q: Does spinach contain much more iron than other vegetables?
a: Yes, it is almost pure iron
100834.e: Fresh spinach contains about as much iron as other green vegetables. Its reputation as an iron wonder is exaggerated.
100834.m: Spinach is not an iron wonder.

100835.q: Where does the wrong high iron figure for spinach probably come from?
a: Dried spinach was measured instead of fresh
Spinach was mixed up with iron
100835.e: Around 1890 a researcher measured the iron content of dried spinach. Others later used the high figure for fresh spinach.
100835.m: Dried spinach led to the iron myth.

100836.q: Which cartoon character gets strong from spinach?
100836.e: Popeye is a sailor from comics and cartoons. When he eats spinach, he gets enormous strength.

100837.q: Can our body absorb the iron from spinach well?
a: Not at all, it is poison
100837.e: Spinach contains substances like oxalic acid that bind the iron. That is why the body only absorbs a small part of it.
100837.m: The iron from spinach is poorly absorbed.

100838.q: What does spinach contain plenty of?
100838.e: Spinach is healthy, even if it isn't an iron wonder. For example, it contains lots of vitamins.

100839.q: Is it all right to reheat cooked spinach?
a: Yes, if it was cooled quickly
100839.e: Cooked spinach should be cooled quickly and kept in the fridge. Then you can reheat it once; for babies it is better to use fresh.
100839.m: Spinach can be reheated after being cooled quickly.

100840.q: What does our body need iron for?
100840.e: Iron is part of the red pigment in blood. This carries oxygen in the blood.
100840.m: The body needs iron for the blood.

100841.q: Which food contains much more iron than fresh spinach?
100841.e: Liver contains much more iron than fresh spinach. Cucumber, apple and milk, on the other hand, contain little iron.

100842.q: Which part of spinach do you eat?
100842.e: Spinach is a leaf vegetable. You eat its green leaves raw or cooked.
100842.m: With spinach you eat the leaves.

100843.q: Does the mole eat plant roots?
100843.e: The mole is a meat-eater. It eats worms and insect larvae, but no roots.

100844.q: Which animal nibbles roots in the garden and is often mistaken for the mole?
100844.e: The water vole is a kind of vole. It eats roots and bulbs, and the damage it does is often blamed on the mole.
100844.m: It is the water vole that eats roots, not the mole.

a: Its sleeping place made of grass
100845.e: When digging, the mole pushes the loose earth upwards. That makes the typical mounds on the meadow.
100845.m: Molehills are earth pushed out of the ground.

100846.q: What does the mole use to dig its tunnels?
100846.e: The mole's front paws are as broad as shovels. With them it quickly digs long tunnels.
100846.m: The mole digs with its shovel paws.

100847.q: What does the mole keep in its larder?
100847.e: The mole paralyses earthworms with a bite and stores them alive. That way it has food even in winter.
100847.m: The mole collects earthworms as a food store.

100848.q: Why can the mole also run backwards in its tunnel?
a: Its fur can be stroked in any direction
It has eyes in the back of its head
It always turns in a circle
100848.e: The mole's velvety fur has no grain. So it doesn't catch on the walls going forwards or backwards.
100848.m: The mole's fur is velvety soft with no grain.

a: No, it is awake in winter too
Yes, but only when it snows
100849.e: The mole doesn't hibernate. In winter it digs deeper, where the ground isn't frozen.
100849.m: The mole is awake in winter too.

100850.q: What does the mole use to detect its prey in the soil?
100850.e: The mole's snout-like nose is very sensitive. With it, it smells and feels worms and larvae.
100850.m: The mole finds prey with its nose.

100851.q: Who comes when you call 144 in Switzerland?
100851.e: The number 144 is the emergency number for the ambulance service. It sends an ambulance with paramedics.
100851.m: When you call 144, the ambulance comes.

100852.q: How much does a call to the emergency number 144 cost?
100852.e: Emergency calls in Switzerland are free. That way everyone can get help straight away.

100853.q: What is especially important to say when you call 144?
100853.e: The rescue team must know where to go. That is why you say exactly where you are.
100853.m: When I make an emergency call, I say exactly where I am.

100855.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland if there is a fire?
100855.e: 118 is the number for the fire brigade. It comes to every fire.
100855.m: If there is a fire, I call the fire brigade on 118.

100856.q: What is the number for the police in Switzerland?
100856.e: You can reach the police on 117. They help, for example, after a burglary.

100857.q: Which number do you call if a child has swallowed something poisonous?
100857.e: 145 is the number of Tox Info Suisse. Experts there help with poisoning around the clock; if someone is unconscious, you dial 144.

100858.q: Are you allowed to call 144 for fun?
100858.e: Anyone who calls for fun blocks the line. Then someone in a real emergency might not get through.
100858.m: I only call the emergency number in an emergency.

100859.q: What kind of help is the number 144 for?
100859.e: 144 is for people who need medical help quickly, for example after an accident.

100860.q: Which emergency number works all over Europe?
100860.e: 112 is the European emergency number. It works in all EU countries and in Switzerland too.

100861.q: Does the number 112 also work in Switzerland?
100861.e: 112 also works in Switzerland. You can get help quickly with it too.

100862.q: When is the number 112 especially useful?
100862.e: Abroad, you often do not know the emergency numbers. 112 is the same in many European countries.
100862.m: On holiday in Europe, I dial 112 in an emergency.

100863.q: How many digits does the European emergency number have?
100863.e: The European emergency number is 112, so one, one, two. That is three digits.
100863.m: The European emergency number has only three digits.

100864.q: Which emergency number is used mainly in the USA?
100864.e: In the USA and Canada, people dial 911. In Europe, it is 112.
100864.m: In Europe I dial 112, and in the USA 911.

100865.q: Who do you reach in Switzerland when you dial 112?
100865.e: If you dial 112, you get through to an emergency control centre. They send the right help.
100865.m: With 112, I reach an emergency control centre.

100866.q: What can you dial the European emergency number 112 for?
100866.e: On 112, they help you with accidents, fire or danger. It does not matter what kind of emergency it is.

100867.q: Can you call 112 with a mobile phone too?
100867.e: 112 works with mobiles and landlines. That is why you can also dial it when you are out and about.
100867.m: I can dial 112 on a mobile phone too.

100868.q: What do you do first with a small graze?
a: Not look at it at all
100868.e: First you wash dirt out of the wound with clean water. Then a plaster goes on.

100869.q: Which part of a plaster should you not touch with your fingers?
a: The soft pad in the middle
The sticky strips on the outside
100869.e: The pad lies directly on the wound. It should stay clean so that no germs get in.
100869.m: I do not touch the pad of a plaster.

100870.q: What is a plaster on a small wound for?
100870.e: The plaster covers the wound. That way less dirt and fewer germs get in.
100870.m: A plaster protects a wound from dirt.

100871.q: Where should plasters be kept at home?
100871.e: In the first aid kit, everything for first aid is in one place. That way you can find it quickly.
100871.m: I keep plasters in the first aid kit.

100872.q: When do you put a new plaster on a wound?
a: When the old one is wet or dirty
When the old one is still completely clean
100872.e: A wet or dirty plaster no longer protects well. Then you put on a new clean plaster.
100872.m: I replace a dirty plaster with a new one.

100873.q: When is a plaster NOT enough any more?
a: When a wound is bleeding heavily
100873.e: For heavy bleeding, you need a bandage and help from adults. A plaster is only for small wounds.
100873.m: If there is heavy bleeding, I get help straight away.

100874.q: What do you do before you put a plaster on someone?
100874.e: Clean hands carry fewer germs to the wound. That is why you wash them first.
100874.m: Before treating a wound, I wash my hands.

100875.q: What can you use to treat a clean wound against germs before putting on a plaster?
100875.e: A disinfectant from the first aid kit kills germs. Then you put the plaster on.
100875.m: Disinfectant kills germs in a wound.

100876.q: What is the wound called when you fall on your knee and scrape the skin?
100876.e: With a graze, the top layer of skin has been rubbed off. It usually only bleeds a little.
100876.m: Scraped skin is called a graze.

100877.q: What is a roll of bandage usually made of?
100877.e: A bandage is made of fabric such as gauze or stretchy material. You can wrap it around a wound.
100877.m: A bandage is made of soft fabric.

100878.q: How tight should a bandage be?
100878.e: A bandage that is too tight cuts off the blood. A bandage that is too loose slips off.
100878.m: A bandage sits firmly, but not too tightly.

100879.q: How can you tell that a bandage on an arm is too tight?
a: The fingers turn blue and cold
The fingers turn warm and pink
100879.e: If too little blood reaches the fingers, they turn blue, cold or tingle. Then the bandage must be loosened.
100879.m: Blue, cold fingers show that a bandage is too tight.

100880.q: What is the cloth called that you can use to support an injured arm?
100880.e: With a triangular bandage, you can make an arm sling. That keeps the injured arm still.
100880.m: I support an arm with a triangular bandage.

100881.q: What do you do first if a wound is bleeding heavily?
a: Press firmly on the wound and get help
Rinse the wound with water and wait
Let the wound dry in the air
Stick a small plaster next to it
100881.e: Pressure on the wound slows the bleeding. At the same time, you get help or call the emergency number 144.
100881.m: With heavy bleeding, press firmly on the wound.

100882.q: Where in Switzerland can you often find a first aid kit?
100882.e: Many cars, schools and sports halls have a first aid kit. It contains bandages and plasters.
100882.m: Schools and cars have first aid kits.

100883.q: Why do you need disposable gloves when putting on a bandage?
a: To protect against blood and germs
100883.e: Gloves protect both helpers and injured people from germs. You find them in the first aid kit.
100883.m: I put on gloves when bandaging.

100884.q: What do you put directly on a wound first, before wrapping it?
100884.e: A sterile dressing lies cleanly on the wound. You wrap the bandage over it.
100884.m: A clean dressing goes on the wound first.

100885.q: What helps straight after spraining your foot?
100885.e: Cooling and raising it make the swelling less bad. Afterwards an adult should check whether you need to see a doctor.
100885.m: I cool a sprained foot and raise it.

100886.q: Why do you never put ice directly on the skin?
100886.e: Ice directly on the skin can cause cold damage. That is why you always wrap it in a cloth.
100886.m: I always wrap ice in a cloth.

100887.q: What do you wrap an ice pack in before putting it on the skin?
100887.e: A thin cloth protects the skin from too much cold. The ice pack still cools well.
100887.m: I only put an ice pack on the skin with a cloth.

100888.q: What can you cool with if there is no ice pack?
100888.e: A cloth with cold water also cools. You make it wet again when it gets warm.
100888.m: A wet, cold cloth also cools well.

100889.q: What does cooling often help with?
100889.e: Cooling helps a bump to swell less. If there is a bad headache or vomiting, you must go to the doctor.

100890.q: What happens when you cool a bruise?
100890.e: Cold makes the blood vessels narrower. Less blood leaks out, so the area swells less.

100891.q: What do you cool a small burn with?
100891.e: Cool but not ice-cold water eases the pain. Ice cubes directly on the skin can do harm.
100891.m: I cool a small burn with water.

100892.q: What do you take out of the freezer when you need to cool something quickly?
100892.e: An ice pack is ready in the freezer. You put it, protected, on the injured area.
100892.m: An ice pack from the freezer helps with bumps.

100893.q: Where do ticks wait for people and animals?
100893.e: Ticks sit on grasses and shrubs. They get brushed off onto you as you walk past.
100893.m: Ticks wait in grass and bushes.

100894.q: What do you do after a trip to the woods?
100894.e: Ticks are small and often bite in warm places. If you check yourself, you find them early.
100894.m: After the woods, I check my body for ticks.

100895.q: What is the best way to remove a tick?
a: With tick tweezers or ordinary tweezers
100895.e: With tick tweezers or ordinary tweezers, you grip the tick close to the skin. Then you pull it out slowly.
100895.m: I pull a tick out with tweezers.

100896.q: When are ticks mainly active in Switzerland?
100896.e: Ticks are active when it is warm enough. That is usually from spring into autumn.
100896.m: Ticks are active from spring to autumn.

100897.q: How many legs does an adult tick have?
100897.e: Adult ticks have four pairs of legs. That makes eight legs.
100897.m: Like spiders, ticks have eight legs.

100898.q: What is best to wear in the woods to protect against ticks?
100898.e: Long trousers and closed shoes protect the skin. Then it is harder for ticks to reach your legs.
100898.m: In the woods, I wear long trousers.

100899.q: How long should you keep an eye on the spot after a tick bite?
100899.e: Illnesses after a tick bite sometimes only show up later. That is why you check the spot for a few weeks.
100899.m: After a tick bite, I watch the spot for a few weeks.

100900.q: What is a warning sign a few days after a tick bite?
a: A red ring that gets bigger
100900.e: A red ring that grows is called a bull's-eye rash. Then you must see a doctor, because it can be an illness.
100900.m: If a red ring is growing, I go to the doctor.

100901.q: What does a tick feed on?
100901.e: Ticks bite people and animals and suck blood. They become much fatter as they do so.

100902.q: What often stays stuck in the skin after a bee sting?
100902.e: A honeybee's sting has tiny barbs. That is why it often stays in the skin along with the venom sac.
100902.m: After a bee sting, the sting is often stuck in the skin.

100903.q: How do you remove a bee sting?
a: Do not remove it at all
100903.e: The most important thing is to remove the sting quickly. It is best to scrape it off sideways with a fingernail.
100903.m: I remove a bee sting quickly.

100904.e: Bees only sting when they feel that they or their colony are under threat. The sting is how they defend themselves.
100904.m: A bee stings when it defends itself.

100905.q: When is a sting in the mouth dangerous?
100905.e: A sting in the mouth or throat can swell so much that it is hard to breathe. Then you dial 144 at once and let the person suck ice.
100905.m: If someone is stung in the mouth, I call 144 at once.

100906.q: What is important if someone has a bee allergy?
100906.e: With an allergy, the whole body can react, for example with difficulty breathing. Then you call the emergency number 144 at once.
100906.m: With an allergy, I get help immediately.

100907.q: How should you behave when a bee is flying around you?
100907.e: Hectic movements make bees nervous. People who stay calm get stung less often.

100908.q: Why should you not drink from open cans of fizzy drink outdoors?
100908.e: Wasps like sweet things and crawl into cans. A sting in the mouth is dangerous, so it is better to drink from a glass or with a straw.
100908.m: Outdoors, I look into my glass before drinking.

100909.q: Which insect usually loses its sting when it stings?
100909.e: The honeybee's sting has barbs and gets stuck. Wasps can pull their sting back out.
100909.m: Only the honeybee usually loses its sting when it stings.

100910.q: Roughly how long should you cool a small burn?
100910.e: Cooling for this long eases the pain and protects the skin. For large burns, you call for help immediately.
100910.m: I cool a burn with water for several minutes.

100911.q: What does NOT belong on a burn?
100911.e: Butter, flour or toothpaste make the wound dirty. They can cause an infection.

100912.q: What do you do with a burn blister?
100912.e: The blister protects the skin underneath from germs. That is why you do not pop it.
100912.m: I do not pop a burn blister.

100913.q: What can you easily burn yourself on in the kitchen?
100913.e: Hobs, pans and the oven get very hot. That is why care is important in the kitchen.
100913.m: I am very careful near the hot cooker.

100914.q: What do you do if a person's clothes are on fire?
a: Get them to roll on the ground and get help
100914.e: Running fans the fire. Rolling on the ground or using a fire blanket smothers the flames, and you call for help at once.
100914.m: Burning clothes are smothered on the ground.

100915.e: Hot liquids or steam injure the skin. This is called a scald.
100915.m: Hot water can scald your skin.

100916.q: What can you cool when you have sunburn?
100916.e: Sunburn is a mild burn of the skin. Cool compresses help against the burning feeling.
100916.m: I cool sunburn with damp cloths.

100917.q: When must you call the emergency number at once for a burn?
100917.e: Large burns are dangerous, especially for children. Then you call 144 at once.

100918.q: What do you do first as a child when there is an accident?
100918.e: Adults are better able to help and can call the emergency number. That is why you fetch someone at once.
100918.m: If there is an accident, I fetch an adult at once.

100919.q: What do you pay attention to before helping at the scene of an accident?
100919.e: If you put yourself in danger, you cannot help anyone. The road, for example, is dangerous.
100919.m: When helping, I look after myself first.

100920.q: Who can you ask for help in the playground?
100920.e: Teachers are on playground duty and know what to do. They can also call for help.
100920.m: In the playground, I fetch the teacher.

100921.q: What do you do while an adult calls the emergency number?
100921.e: An injured person is often frightened. If someone stays with them and talks to them, it calms them down.
100921.m: I stay with injured people and comfort them.

100922.q: What can you say to an injured person?
100922.e: Calming words make people feel safer. The person then knows that someone will come soon.
100922.m: I calm injured people with kind words.

100923.q: What do you do if there is no adult nearby?
100923.e: Children may and should call the emergency number too. The control centre will tell you exactly what you can do.
100923.m: Even as a child, I may call the emergency number.

100924.q: How do you call loudly for help?
100924.e: Other people hear loud, clear shouting more quickly. Then they come to help.
100924.m: I call for help loudly and clearly.

100925.q: Which address should you know by heart for emergencies?
a: The address of the zoo in Paris
The address of a toy shop
100925.e: When you make an emergency call, you must say where you are. If you know your address, you can quickly get help to your home.
100925.m: I know my address by heart.

100926.q: What do you tell an adult that you fetch to help?
100926.e: The adult must quickly know what is going on and where to go. That way they can help straight away.
100926.m: I say briefly what has happened and where.

100927.q: What is the phone number of Rega?
100927.e: Rega, the Swiss Air Rescue service, can be reached on 1414.

100928.q: How does Rega usually reach injured people?
100928.e: Rega flies rescue helicopters. That way it can quickly reach places in the mountains too.

100929.e: Rega helicopters are red and white. That makes them easy to spot in the sky.
100929.m: Rega helicopters are red and white.

100930.e: Rega rescues people in need with helicopters and air ambulance jets. It has existed since 1952.
100930.m: Rega is the Swiss Air Rescue service.

100932.q: What are the people called who support Rega with a yearly contribution?
100932.e: Rega gets a lot of money from its patrons. That way it can pay for its helicopters.

100933.q: Where does the Rega helicopter help especially often?
100933.e: In the mountains, the journey by car takes a long time. The helicopter is much faster there.
100933.m: Rega often helps in the mountains.

100934.q: Who is on board the helicopter during a Rega mission?
100934.e: The crew includes a pilot, a paramedic and an emergency doctor. That way they can help injured people right on the spot.
100934.m: A doctor flies on the Rega helicopter.

100935.q: What does an ambulance switch on during an emergency journey?
100935.e: Blue lights and the siren warn others. They should clear the way.
100935.m: When I see blue lights and hear a siren, I make way.

100936.q: What do you do on your bike when an ambulance comes with its siren on?
a: Stay in the middle of the road
100936.e: Emergency vehicles need a clear road. Stopping at the side helps them.
100936.m: When an ambulance comes, I make way.

100938.e: Paramedics look after people who are ill or injured. They take them to hospital.

100939.q: Where does the ambulance usually take injured people?
100939.e: In hospital, doctors continue to treat the injured.
100939.m: The ambulance takes injured people to hospital.

100940.q: What is on board an ambulance?
100940.e: An ambulance has bandages, medicines and equipment. With these, the paramedics can help on the way.
100940.m: An ambulance carries equipment to help injured people.

100941.q: Why is the word “AMBULANCE” written back to front on the front of some ambulances?
a: So it can be read in the rear-view mirror
100941.e: A driver sees everything mirrored in the rear-view mirror. That way they read the word the right way round.
100941.m: Mirror writing can be read correctly in a rear-view mirror.

100942.q: May an ambulance with blue lights and siren drive through a red light at a junction?
100942.e: In an emergency, rescue vehicles with blue lights and siren may ignore traffic rules. But they must drive carefully.
100942.m: An ambulance on an emergency may carefully drive through a red light.

100943.q: What does a foil emergency blanket usually look like?
100943.e: An emergency blanket is a thin foil. One side shines gold, the other silver.
100943.m: An emergency blanket shines gold and silver.

100944.q: What is an emergency blanket mainly for?
a: It replaces an umbrella on walks
100944.e: Injured people get cold quickly. The foil keeps warmth near the body and protects against wind and wet.
100944.m: An emergency blanket keeps injured people warm.

100945.q: How thick is an emergency blanket?
100945.e: An emergency blanket is a wafer-thin foil. That is why, folded up, it fits into any small bag.
100945.m: An emergency blanket is as thin as foil.

100946.q: Where can you find an emergency blanket?
100946.e: Emergency blankets belong in first aid kits and hiking first aid packs.
100946.m: There is an emergency blanket in the first aid kit.

100947.q: Why do you pack an emergency blanket for a mountain hike?
a: Because it is light and small
Because it shines like a lamp
100947.e: An emergency blanket weighs almost nothing. In an emergency in the mountains, it protects against cold.
100947.m: An emergency blanket is light and fits into any rucksack.

100948.q: What do you do with an emergency blanket for an injured person?
a: Fan air at them with it
100948.e: You wrap the injured person loosely, leaving the face free. That way they lose less heat.
100948.m: I cover injured people with an emergency blanket.

100949.q: What else does the shiny emergency blanket help with?
a: Rescuers can see it from far away
100949.e: The shiny foil reflects light. That makes it easier to find injured people, for example from a helicopter.
100949.m: The shiny emergency blanket can be seen from far away.

100950.q: What is an emergency blanket made of?
100950.e: It is made of a thin plastic foil with a wafer-thin layer of metal. That is why it shines.
100950.m: An emergency blanket is made of shiny foil.

100951.q: What does rain fall to the Earth from?
100951.e: Tiny water droplets gather in clouds. When they get big enough, they fall down as rain.

100952.q: Why do drops of water fall out of a cloud?
100952.e: Small droplets float in the air. When they grow together into big drops, they are too heavy and fall.

100953.q: What do you call very fine, light rain?
100953.e: In drizzle, very small droplets fall. You can hardly feel them.

100954.q: What do you call sudden, very heavy rain?
100954.e: In a downpour, a lot of water falls in a short time. It often comes with a thunderstorm.
100954.m: A downpour is short and very heavy.

100955.q: What shape are falling raindrops really?
100955.e: Small raindrops are almost perfectly round. Big drops get squashed a little flat at the bottom as they fall.
100955.m: Raindrops are not pointed but almost round.

100956.q: Where does rainwater on the road flow to?
100956.e: At the side of the road there are drains with grates. The water flows through them into the sewers.
100956.m: Rainwater flows through drains into the sewers.

100957.q: What is the journey of water from the sea into the clouds and back as rain called?
100957.e: Water evaporates, forms clouds and falls back to the Earth as rain. This happens again and again.
100957.m: Water keeps travelling round the water cycle.

100958.q: How many arms does a snowflake usually have?
100958.e: Snow crystals usually grow with six arms. This is because of the way ice is built.

100959.e: Snowflakes are frozen water. Lots of small ice crystals are stuck together.
100959.m: Snowflakes are made of ice crystals.

100960.q: What can slide down when there is a lot of snow on a steep slope?
100960.e: An avalanche is snow that slides down a slope. It can be very dangerous.
100960.m: Lots of snow on a steep slope can slide down as an avalanche.

100961.q: Where in Switzerland is there snow even in summer?
100961.e: High up in the Alps it is so cold that snow can stay on the ground in summer. There are glaciers there too.
100961.m: On high mountains there is snow even in summer.

100962.q: What do you call rain and snow falling together?
100962.e: When the temperature is just above zero, some flakes melt. Then rain and snow fall mixed together.
100962.m: Sleet is rain mixed with snow.

100963.q: At what temperature does snow settle well?
100963.e: If it is warmer, the snow melts quickly. At zero degrees or below it settles.
100963.m: Snow settles when it is cold enough.

100964.q: Why does snow crunch under your shoes when it is very cold?
100964.e: When it is very cold, the ice crystals are hard. When you step on them, they break, and that crunches.
100964.m: Breaking ice crystals make snow crunch.

100965.q: What do you call loose, dry snow that cannot be made into snowballs?
100965.e: Powder snow is very dry and light. That is why it does not stick together well.
100965.m: Dry powder snow does not stick together well.

100966.q: How big can very large hailstones get?
a: As big as a tennis ball
100966.e: Hailstones are usually smaller than a pea. But in strong thunderstorms they can be as big as a tennis ball.
100966.m: Hailstones can get very big in strong thunderstorms.

100967.e: Large hailstones are hard and heavy. They dent cars and destroy roof tiles and plants.
100967.m: Large hail can damage cars and roofs.

100968.q: Where do you go when it hails?
100968.e: Hailstones can hurt and injure you. Indoors you are protected.
100968.m: When it hails, I go indoors.

100969.q: What do farmers stretch over fruit trees to protect them from hail?
100969.e: Hail nets catch the ice stones. That way apples and cherries stay undamaged.

100970.q: What do you often see if you cut open a large hailstone?
100970.e: A hailstone is carried up and down in the cloud several times. Each time, a new layer of ice freezes onto it.

100971.q: What are small, soft little balls of ice that look like polystyrene called?
100971.e: Graupel is small, soft pellets of ice and snow. It is softer than hail.

100972.q: What happens to hailstones on a warm summer's day after the thunderstorm?
100972.e: Hail is ice. In the warm air it quickly melts into water.
100972.m: Hail melts into water in the warmth.

100973.q: What are white, round clouds that look like balls of cotton wool called?
100973.e: Cumulus clouds have a flat bottom and round tops. You often see them in fine weather.
100973.m: Cumulus clouds look like cotton wool.

100974.q: What are very high, thin and wispy clouds called?
100974.e: Cirrus clouds are right up high in the sky. They are made of ice crystals.
100974.m: Cirrus clouds float very high up.

100975.q: What moves the clouds across the sky?
100975.e: Clouds float in the air. The wind pushes them along.

100976.q: What is the white stripe behind a high-flying aeroplane called?
100976.e: The exhaust gases contain water vapour. It freezes in the cold air into a white stripe of ice crystals.

100977.q: What can happen when very tall towers of cloud form in the afternoon?
100977.e: Tall towers of cloud grow quickly on warm days. A thunderstorm can develop from them.
100977.m: Tall cloud towers warn of a thunderstorm.

100978.q: What are clouds that cover the whole sky like a grey blanket called?
100978.e: Stratus clouds are flat and wide. The sky then looks grey.
100978.m: Stratus clouds make the sky grey.

100979.q: What is the scale used to give wind strength called?
100979.e: The Beaufort scale divides the wind into levels. It is named after Francis Beaufort.
100979.m: Wind strength is given on the Beaufort scale.

100980.q: What number is calm on the Beaufort scale?
100980.e: At force 0 the air hardly moves. Smoke rises straight up.

100981.q: What is the highest wind force on the Beaufort scale?
100981.e: The Beaufort scale goes from 0 to 12. Force 12 is the strongest wind.
100981.m: The Beaufort scale goes up to 12.

100982.q: What is the strongest wind, force 12, called?
100982.e: A hurricane-force wind is an extremely strong storm. It can uproot trees and rip roofs off.
100982.m: Hurricane force is the strongest wind.

100983.q: How can you tell there is a light wind?
100983.e: In a light wind, leaves rustle and small twigs move. Big branches stay still.
100983.m: In a light wind the leaves move.

100984.q: What do you call sudden, short, strong bursts of wind?
100984.e: Gusts are short bursts of wind. They are stronger than the wind before and after.
100984.m: Gusts are sudden bursts of wind.

100985.q: In which unit does the weather forecast often give the wind speed?
100985.e: Wind speed is given in kilometres per hour, just like for a car.
100985.m: Wind speed is measured in kilometres per hour.

100986.q: What do you call a gentle, pleasant wind?
100986.e: A breeze is a light wind. By the sea or a lake it cools you down on hot days.
100986.m: A breeze is a gentle wind.

100987.q: Which animal often sits on top of a weather vane on a church tower?
100987.e: Many weather vanes are shaped like a cockerel. That is why they are also called weathercocks.
100987.m: On many church towers a weathercock turns.

100988.q: Why does a weather vane turn?
100988.e: The wide surface of the vane catches the wind. The wind turns it until it lines up with the wind.
100988.m: The wind turns the weather vane.

100989.q: Which letters are often found under a weather vane?
100989.e: The letters stand for north, east, south and west. That way you can see the wind direction exactly.
100989.m: N, E, S and W are the four points of the compass.

100990.q: The point of a weather vane is pointing west. Where is the wind coming from?
100990.e: The point of a weather vane points in the direction the wind is coming from. So here it is coming from the west.
100990.m: The point of a weather vane shows where the wind comes from.

100991.q: What can a weather vane NOT show?
100991.e: A weather vane only shows the direction of the wind. For the temperature you need a thermometer.
100991.m: A weather vane shows wind direction, not temperature.

100992.q: What material are weather vanes on roofs usually made of?
100992.e: Weather vanes stand outside in wind and rain for years. Metal can stand up to that well.
100992.m: Weather vanes are usually made of metal.

100993.q: Why is a weather vane right at the top of the roof?
a: So that birds can sit on it
100993.e: Lower down, houses and trees slow the wind. Right at the top the wind can blow freely.
100993.m: A weather vane stands high so that the wind can reach it freely.

100994.q: What does a weather vane do when there is no wind?
100994.e: Without wind there is nothing to turn the vane. It simply stays still.
100994.m: Without wind a weather vane stays still.

100995.q: In which unit is the amount of rain given?
100995.e: You measure how high the water is in the rain gauge. That is why the amount of rain is given in millimetres.
100995.m: The amount of rain is measured in millimetres.

100996.q: How much water is 1 millimetre of rain on one square metre?
100996.e: One millimetre of rain means that one litre of water falls on every square metre of ground.
100996.m: One millimetre of rain is one litre per square metre.

100997.q: On Monday 3 millimetres of rain fall, on Tuesday 5 millimetres. How much is that altogether?
100997.e: You add the amounts of rain together: 3 + 5 = 8 millimetres.
100997.m: Add up the rain from several days.

100998.q: What must you do with a rain gauge after reading it?
100998.e: After reading it, you pour the water out. That way you can measure the next rain from the start.
100998.m: After reading it, I empty the rain gauge.

100999.q: What can you use to make a simple rain gauge yourself?
a: A straight-sided glass with a scale
100999.e: A glass with straight sides collects the water. With a scale in millimetres you read off the amount.
100999.m: A straight glass with a scale is a simple rain gauge.

101000.q: What is another name for a rain gauge?
101000.e: A rain gauge also measures snow and hail. That is why it has another name too.
101000.m: A rain gauge is also called a precipitation gauge.

101001.q: Which canton is often called the ‘sun parlour of Switzerland’?
101001.e: Ticino lies south of the Alps. The sun shines often there and it is mild.
101001.m: Ticino is called the sun parlour of Switzerland.

101002.q: Why are there more hours of sunshine in summer than in winter?
101002.e: In summer the sun rises early and sets late. So it can shine for many hours.
101002.m: In summer the days are long.

101003.q: In which unit do you give how long the sun shone on a day?
101003.e: This is called the hours of sunshine. It is given in hours.

101004.q: What often lies over the Central Plateau in winter while the sun shines in the mountains?
101004.e: Cold, damp air stays down in the valley and forms fog. From above it looks like a sea.
101004.m: Above the sea of fog the sun often shines.

101005.q: Which picture in the weather forecast shows fine, sunny weather?
101005.e: The weather forecast uses pictures for the weather. The yellow sun means sunshine.
101005.m: The yellow sun stands for sunshine.

101006.q: What does the word ‘fair’ mean in the weather forecast?
101006.e: Fair means that the sun shines a lot. There are only a few clouds in the sky.
101006.m: Fair weather is sunny with few clouds.

101007.q: On which day of the year do we have the longest day of sunlight?
101007.e: Summer begins around 21 June. That is when the sun shines longest here.
101007.m: The longest day is in June.

101008.q: What do you call the sky when not a single cloud can be seen?
101008.e: A cloudless sky is completely blue. Then the sun can shine without anything in the way.
101008.m: A cloudless sky is completely blue.

101009.q: What does the UV index in the weather forecast show?
a: How strong the sun's radiation is
101009.e: The UV index tells you how much the sun can harm your skin. When the value is high, you protect yourself especially well.
101009.m: A high UV index means strong sun radiation.

101010.q: On which nights is frost most likely?
101010.e: Without clouds, the warmth of the ground escapes into the sky. That is why it gets especially cold on clear nights.

101011.q: What does frost paint on cold window panes?
101011.e: Moisture freezes into patterns on the cold pane. They look like flowers made of ice.
101011.m: Frost paints ice flowers on the window.

101012.q: Why can a full glass bottle of water burst in a frost?
a: Ice needs more room than water
101012.e: When water freezes, it expands. The ice pushes the bottle apart.

101013.q: What is spread on icy pavements in winter?
101013.e: Salt makes the ice melt, and grit makes the ground rough. That way you slip less.
101013.m: Salt or grit is spread against ice.

101014.q: How do you protect delicate plants from frost?
a: Cut them off and throw them away
101014.e: A fleece keeps the warmth of the ground near the plants. That way they are less likely to freeze.
101014.m: A fleece protects plants from frost.

101015.q: What are the days in mid-May called, after which little frost is expected?
101015.e: According to an old farmers' saying, there can still be frost up to the Ice Saints in mid-May. That is why delicate plants are often only planted after that.
101015.m: After the Ice Saints, delicate plants are planted out.

101016.q: What is ground in the Alps that stays frozen all year round called?
101016.e: High in the mountains the ground is so cold that it stays frozen even in summer. This is called permafrost.
101016.m: Permafrost stays frozen all year round.

101017.q: Where does the road often get slippery first in a frost?
101017.e: Cold air flows around bridges from below and above. That is why they freeze earlier than the normal road.
101017.m: In a frost, bridges are often slippery first.

101018.q: What is the air usually like when the föhn blows?
101018.e: The föhn comes down the mountains and warms up as it does. The air becomes warm and dry.
101018.m: The föhn brings warm, dry air.

101019.q: Over which mountains does the föhn come into northern Switzerland?
101019.e: The föhn blows from the south over the Alps. Then it drops down into the valleys on the north side.
101019.m: The föhn comes over the Alps.

101020.q: Which valley in Switzerland is known for the föhn?
101020.e: The Reuss valley in Uri is a typical föhn valley. The Rhine valley and the Hasli valley also often have föhn.
101020.m: The Reuss valley in Uri is a föhn valley.

101021.q: Why is fire especially dangerous when the föhn blows?
a: Wind and dry air spread it fast
The föhn puts out every fire
Fire does not burn in the föhn
101021.e: The dry, strong wind fans the flames. In the past, villages in föhn valleys even kept a föhn watch.
101021.m: When the föhn blows, I do not light fires outdoors.

101022.q: What do some people feel when the föhn blows?
101022.e: Some people are sensitive to the föhn. They get a headache or feel tired when it blows.
101022.m: Some people get headaches when the föhn blows.

101023.q: What is the weather often like on the south side of the Alps when the föhn blows in the north?
101023.e: The air drops its rain on the south side of the Alps. Afterwards it comes down dry into the northern valleys.
101023.m: When the föhn blows in the north, it often rains in the south.

101024.q: What does the föhn do to the snow?
101024.e: The warm föhn melts snow very quickly. That is why it is also called the ‘snow eater’.
101024.m: The föhn eats up the snow.

101025.q: In which seasons does the föhn blow especially often?
101025.e: The föhn is most common in spring, and often in autumn too. It blows less often in summer.
101025.m: The föhn often blows in spring and autumn.

101026.q: What is the wall of cloud you often see over the main ridge of the Alps when the föhn blows called?
101026.e: When the föhn blows, thick clouds often hang on the main ridge of the Alps. From the north they look like a wall.
101026.m: When the föhn blows, there is often a föhn wall over the Alps.

101027.q: What does a falling barometer often show?
101027.e: When the air pressure falls, clouds and rain often come. That is why a barometer helps to forecast the weather.
101027.m: A falling barometer often announces bad weather.

101028.e: The Italian Evangelista Torricelli built the first barometer around 1643. He used a glass tube.

101029.q: Which liquid was in Torricelli's first barometer?
101029.e: Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury. Depending on the air pressure, it stood higher or lower.
101029.m: The first barometer was filled with mercury.

101030.q: Which word is written in the middle of many household barometers?
101030.e: Old barometers have words such as ‘Rain’, ‘Change’ and ‘Fair’. The middle says ‘Change’.
101030.m: The middle of a barometer says ‘Change’.

101031.q: Where is the air pressure lower?
101031.e: On a mountain there is less air above you. That is why the barometer shows a lower air pressure there.
101031.m: On high mountains the air pressure is lower.

101032.q: In which unit is air pressure given in the weather forecast?
101032.e: Air pressure is given in hectopascals, hPa for short. At sea level it is about 1013 hPa on average.
101032.m: Air pressure is measured in hectopascals.

101033.q: What moves on a dial barometer when the air pressure changes?
101033.e: Inside the barometer there is a thin metal capsule. The air pressure squeezes it, and it moves the pointer.
101033.m: The pointer shows the air pressure.

101034.q: What presses on us from all sides all the time without us noticing?
101034.e: There is a thick layer of air above us. Its weight presses on everything, and this is called air pressure.
101034.m: The air is always pressing on us.

101035.q: What is Switzerland's weather service called?
101035.e: MeteoSwiss is the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology. It makes the official weather forecasts.

101036.q: Where do you have to measure the air temperature to get it right?
101036.e: In the sun, the thermometer itself heats up. That is why the air temperature is measured in the shade.
101036.m: Air temperature is measured in the shade.

101037.q: What does the weather forecast mean by ‘precipitation’?
101037.e: Precipitation is all the water that falls from the sky. It includes rain, snow and hail.
101037.m: Precipitation is water that falls from the sky.

101038.q: In which unit does the weather forecast in Switzerland give the temperature?
101038.e: In Switzerland temperature is measured in degrees Celsius. Water freezes at zero degrees.
101038.m: Temperature is given in degrees Celsius.

101039.q: What does a 90 per cent chance of rain mean?
101039.e: The number shows how likely rain is. 90 per cent means very likely, so take an umbrella.
101039.m: When the chance of rain is high, I take an umbrella.

101040.q: What do weather satellites provide for the weather forecast?
a: Pictures of the clouds from above
101040.e: Weather satellites circle high above the Earth. They photograph the clouds so that the weather can be forecast.
101040.m: Weather satellites photograph the clouds from above.

101041.q: How many danger levels do severe weather warnings have in Switzerland?
101041.e: The warnings go from level 1 to level 5. The higher the level, the more dangerous the weather.
101041.m: Severe weather warnings in Switzerland have five levels.

101042.q: In German, what is a weather forecaster jokingly called?
101042.e: In German, people who forecast the weather are jokingly called ‘weather frogs’. In the past, people believed that tree frogs could show what the weather would be.
101042.m: In German, a ‘weather frog’ jokingly forecasts the weather.

101043.q: What do you call an expert who studies and forecasts the weather?
101043.e: Meteorologists study the weather. They produce the weather forecast.

101044.q: Which three space agencies jointly ran the Cassini-Huygens mission?
101044.e: Cassini was built by NASA and the Huygens lander by ESA, and the Italian space agency ASI supplied the high-gain antenna, among other things.
101044.m: Cassini-Huygens was a joint project of NASA, ESA and ASI.

101045.q: For how long after Huygens landed on Titan did Cassini still receive data from the surface?
101045.e: Huygens worked on batteries and radioed to the Earth via Cassini. After Cassini disappeared below the horizon, no more surface data arrived after about 72 minutes.
101045.m: Huygens delivered data from Titan’s surface for a good hour.

101046.q: Why was Cassini deliberately steered into Saturn’s atmosphere on 15 September 2017?
a: So as not to contaminate Enceladus and Titan with microbes from Earth
Because the solar panels no longer supplied power
Because the probe was too heavy for the return flight
To create a new ring of Saturn
101046.e: The propellant was running low, and an uncontrolled probe could later have crashed onto a moon that might be hospitable to life. The deliberate crash served planetary protection.
101046.m: Cassini burnt up in Saturn in 2017 so that its moons stayed clean.

101047.q: Which technique did Cassini use to reach Saturn without huge amounts of propellant?
a: Swing-by manoeuvres at Venus, the Earth and Jupiter
A solar sail all the way to Saturn
A second rocket stage in Earth orbit
101047.e: Cassini flew past Venus twice, the Earth once and Jupiter once, gaining speed each time. This technique is called a swing-by or gravity assist.
101047.m: Cassini picked up momentum at Venus, the Earth and Jupiter.

101048.q: How was Cassini supplied with electrical energy?
a: With large areas of solar panels
101048.e: At Saturn’s distance, sunlight is about a hundred times weaker than at the Earth. Three radioisotope generators turned the decay heat of plutonium-238 into electricity.
101048.m: Cassini got its power from the decay of plutonium.

101049.q: What did Cassini discover on the surface of Titan?
a: Lakes of liquid methane and ethane
101049.e: Radar images showed lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons in Titan’s polar regions. Besides the Earth, Titan is thus the only known body with stable liquids on its surface.
101049.m: On Titan there are lakes of methane and ethane.

101050.q: What was the last phase of the Cassini mission called, with 22 orbits between Saturn and its rings?
101050.e: From April 2017, Cassini flew 22 times through the gap between the innermost ring and Saturn’s atmosphere. In the process, the gravity field and the mass of the rings were measured precisely.
101050.m: In the Grand Finale, Cassini dived 22 times between Saturn and its rings.

101051.q: In which year did Cassini reach orbit around Saturn?
101051.e: Cassini was launched in October 1997 and swung into orbit around Saturn on 1 July 2004. The mission there lasted more than 13 years.

101052.q: How does Juno’s power supply differ from earlier Jupiter probes such as Galileo?
a: Juno uses solar panels instead of radioisotope generators
Juno uses fuel cells instead of solar panels
Juno uses a small nuclear reactor
Juno is supplied from the Earth by laser
101052.e: Juno is the first probe to work at Jupiter on solar power alone. For this it has three large solar wings.
101052.m: Juno flies at Jupiter on solar energy.

101053.q: What kind of orbit does Juno fly around Jupiter?
a: An orbit at the Lagrange point L1
101053.e: The elliptical polar orbit takes Juno very close above the clouds while avoiding the strongest parts of the radiation belts. This limits the radiation dose per orbit.
101053.m: Juno orbits Jupiter over the poles on an elongated orbit.

101054.q: Why does a Juno orbit take about 53 days instead of the 14 days originally planned?
a: Because of problems with valves of the main engine
Because Jupiter is heavier than calculated
Because a solar wing broke off
Because of a collision with a moon
101054.e: Before the planned orbit manoeuvre in 2016, helium valves of the engine showed a fault. NASA therefore gave up shortening the orbital period.
101054.m: A valve problem left Juno on the long 53-day orbit.

101055.q: What is the titanium box inside Juno for?
a: It protects the electronics from radiation
It serves as a heat store for the night
101055.e: The titanium vault, about a centimetre thick, shields the sensitive electronics from the high-energy particles in Jupiter’s magnetic field. Without it, the electronics would quickly be damaged.
101055.m: A titanium vault protects Juno’s electronics from Jupiter’s radiation.

101056.q: What did Juno’s gravity measurements show about Jupiter’s core?
a: It is diluted and not sharply bounded
Jupiter has no rocky interior at all
101056.e: The data point to a large, diluted core in which heavy elements are mixed with hydrogen. This contradicted the picture of a small, compact rocky core.
101056.m: According to Juno, Jupiter’s core is more blurred than compact.

101057.q: On what date did Juno swing into orbit around Jupiter?
101057.e: Juno was launched on 5 August 2011 and reached Jupiter on 4 July 2016. The date fell on the American national holiday.
101057.m: Juno arrived at Jupiter on 4 July 2016.

101058.q: Which moon of Jupiter did Juno fly particularly close to at the end of 2023 and the start of 2024, to observe its volcanoes?
101058.e: Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System. Juno passed it in December 2023 and in February 2024 at a height of about 1500 kilometres.
101058.m: Juno visited the volcanic moon Io up close.

101059.q: What does the name Juno signify in relation to the planet Jupiter?
a: In Roman mythology, Juno is Jupiter’s wife
Juno is a moon of Jupiter
Juno is the discoverer of the Great Red Spot
Juno is the discoverer of Jupiter’s rings
101059.e: According to the legend, Jupiter wrapped himself in clouds, but his wife Juno could see through them. The probe is meant to look beneath the cloud cover in the same way.
101059.m: Like the goddess, Juno looks beneath Jupiter’s clouds.

101060.q: About how long did the radio signals from New Horizons take to reach the Earth during the Pluto flyby in 2015?
101060.e: Pluto was then about 33 astronomical units, or about 4.9 billion kilometres, away. At the speed of light, that gives a travel time of about 4.5 hours.
101060.m: Signals from Pluto were on their way for over four hours.

101061.q: Which object in the Kuiper Belt did New Horizons visit on 1 January 2019?
101061.e: Arrokoth, formerly called 2014 MU69, is the most distant object ever explored up close by a probe. It consists of two merged parts.
101061.m: Arrokoth is the farthest object ever visited.

101062.q: What shape does the Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth have?
a: Two gently joined bodies (a contact binary)
101062.e: Arrokoth consists of two flat lobes that touched slowly and merged. This points to a gentle origin in the early Solar System.
101062.m: Arrokoth is a contact binary of two bodies.

101063.q: What is the heart-shaped plain Sputnik Planitia on Pluto?
a: A basin full of nitrogen ice
A lava field of silicate rock
A dune landscape of water-ice sand
101063.e: Sputnik Planitia is filled with nitrogen ice, which is divided into polygonal cells by convection. As no craters are visible, the surface is geologically young.
101063.m: Pluto’s heart consists of young nitrogen ice.

101064.q: What special item does New Horizons carry on board?
a: Part of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh
A copy of the Federal Constitution
101064.e: Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930. A small container with his ashes is flying into space with the probe.
101064.m: Pluto’s discoverer Clyde Tombaugh travels along on New Horizons.

101065.q: What status did Pluto have when New Horizons was launched in January 2006, and what changed in the same year?
a: It was a planet and became a dwarf planet in August 2006
It was a moon and became a planet
It was an asteroid and became a comet
It was a dwarf planet and became a planet
101065.e: In August 2006, the International Astronomical Union laid down a new definition of a planet. Pluto does not meet the criterion of having cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.
101065.m: In 2006, Pluto went from being a planet to a dwarf planet.

101066.q: Why did New Horizons fly close past Jupiter in February 2007?
a: To gain momentum through a swing-by
To scoop propellant from the atmosphere
101066.e: The flyby increased the speed by about 4 kilometres per second and shortened the journey to Pluto by about three years.
101066.m: Jupiter’s gravity accelerated New Horizons on its way to Pluto.

101067.q: Which moon of Pluto is the largest and forms almost a double system with Pluto?
101067.e: Charon has about half the diameter of Pluto. The common centre of mass lies outside Pluto, which is why people speak of a double system.
101067.m: Pluto and Charon orbit a centre of mass between them.

101068.q: Which two space agencies operate the Mercury mission BepiColombo?
101068.e: ESA built the Mercury Planetary Orbiter and the Japanese agency JAXA the magnetospheric orbiter Mio. Both travel to Mercury together.
101068.m: BepiColombo is a mission of Europe and Japan.

101069.q: After whom is the BepiColombo mission named?
101069.e: Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo explained the 3:2 resonance of Mercury’s rotation and orbit, and proposed several Mercury flybys for Mariner 10.
101069.m: BepiColombo honours the mathematician Giuseppe Colombo.

101070.q: Which BepiColombo instrument was developed largely at the University of Bern?
101070.e: BELA measures the height of Mercury’s surface with laser pulses. It was built by the University of Bern together with the DLR.
101070.m: The Bernese laser altimeter BELA surveys Mercury’s relief.

101071.q: When is BepiColombo due to swing into orbit around Mercury according to current planning (as of 2025)?
101071.e: From April 2024, the ion engines no longer delivered full power. ESA re-planned the trajectory, so that the arrival shifted by eleven months from December 2025 to November 2026.
101071.m: After a delay, BepiColombo reaches Mercury in November 2026.

101072.q: Which propulsion system does BepiColombo’s transfer module MTM mainly use?
101072.e: The Mercury Transfer Module generates electricity with solar panels and uses it to accelerate xenon ions. These engines deliver little thrust, but over a long time.
101072.m: Ion engines carry BepiColombo slowly but steadily to Mercury.

101073.q: Roughly how long does BepiColombo’s journey last from launch to swinging into Mercury’s orbit?
101073.e: The launch was in October 2018, and the arrival is planned for November 2026. Nine flybys of the Earth, Venus and Mercury slow the probe down step by step.
101073.m: The way into Mercury’s orbit takes about eight years because of many braking manoeuvres.

101074.q: Why is it difficult in terms of energy to put a probe into orbit around Mercury?
a: It has to shed a great deal of orbital energy because it accelerates strongly towards the Sun
Mercury has an extremely dense atmosphere
Mercury spins faster than any other planet
101074.e: When falling towards the Sun, a probe gains a lot of speed. To be captured by Mercury, it has to be slowed down strongly, which takes a lot of propellant or many flybys.
101074.m: Getting to Mercury mostly means braking hard.

101075.q: On which rocket was BepiColombo launched in October 2018?
101075.e: BepiColombo lifted off on 20 October 2018 from the space centre at Kourou in French Guiana on an Ariane 5.
101075.m: BepiColombo was launched on an Ariane 5 in 2018.

101076.q: What does the abbreviation JUICE stand for?
101076.e: JUICE is to explore the icy moons of Jupiter, Ganymede, Europa and Callisto, beneath whose ice oceans are suspected.
101076.m: JUICE explores the ice moons of Jupiter.

101077.q: How many close flybys of Europa are planned in JUICE’s mission plan?
101077.e: JUICE concentrates on Ganymede and Callisto and flies close past Europa only twice. The intensive exploration of Europa is taken on by Europa Clipper.
101077.m: JUICE visits Europa up close only twice.

101078.q: Which planet did JUICE fly past at the end of August 2025 for a swing-by?
101078.e: The flyby of Venus on 31 August 2025 gave JUICE extra momentum. A flyby of the Earth followed in September 2026, and another is planned for 2029.
101078.m: JUICE picked up momentum at Venus in 2025.

101079.q: Which JUICE instrument was developed at the University of Bern?
a: The neutral gas and ion mass spectrometer NIM
101079.e: NIM belongs to the particle package PEP and analyses gases and ions in the thin atmosphere of Jupiter’s moons. The University of Bern built it.
101079.m: The mass spectrometer NIM from Bern sniffs at Jupiter’s moons.

101080.q: When was JUICE launched into space?
101080.e: JUICE was launched on 14 April 2023 on an Ariane 5 from Kourou. The arrival at Jupiter is planned for July 2031.
101080.m: JUICE has been on its way since April 2023.

101081.q: Which manoeuvre did JUICE carry out in August 2024, the first probe ever to do so?
a: A double flyby of the Moon and the Earth
An orbit of the Sun close to the Earth
A braking manoeuvre in Venus’s atmosphere
101081.e: JUICE flew past the Moon on 19 August 2024 and past the Earth a day later. This double flyby saved a lot of propellant.
101081.m: In 2024, JUICE was the first probe to use a Moon-Earth double flyby.

101082.q: Why does JUICE need such large solar panels, about 85 square metres?
a: At Jupiter, sunlight is about 25 times weaker than at the Earth
Because the probe needs a lot of electricity to heat its engines
Because Jupiter strongly absorbs the light
Because the solar cells also serve as a heat shield
101082.e: Jupiter is about five times as far from the Sun as the Earth. Radiation intensity falls with the square of the distance, that is, to about a twenty-fifth.
101082.m: At Jupiter, only about a twenty-fifth of the sunlight arrives.

101083.q: How does JUICE intend to look beneath the ice layer of Jupiter’s moons?
101083.e: The radar RIME can look into the ice to a depth of about 9 kilometres. In this way, layers and possible pockets of water are to be detected.
101083.m: Radar waves probe the ice of Jupiter’s moons.

101084.q: On which space probe does the Bernese camera CaSSIS fly?
101084.e: CaSSIS is the camera system of the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter of ESA and Roscosmos, which was launched in 2016 and reached Mars in the same year.
101084.m: CaSSIS photographs Mars from the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

101085.q: What does the abbreviation CaSSIS stand for?
a: Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System
Camera for Space Science and Investigation Studies
Colour Analysis of Soil and Surface Ice System
101085.e: The name describes the camera’s two strengths. It delivers colour images and can take stereo pairs for height models.
101085.m: CaSSIS takes colour stereo images of the surface of Mars.

101086.q: Which university led the development of CaSSIS?
101086.e: The Physics Institute of the University of Bern, under Nicolas Thomas, led the project. The University of Bern has long experience with space instruments.
101086.m: CaSSIS was developed at the University of Bern.

101087.q: How does CaSSIS produce stereo images of an area?
a: The telescope is rotated to image the area from the front and from behind
Two cameras sit side by side
The probe flies past twice, a year apart
A laser measures each image point individually
101087.e: The telescope sits on a rotating mechanism. It images an area first obliquely forwards and seconds later obliquely backwards, which gives two viewing angles.
101087.m: CaSSIS rotates to see an area from two angles.

101088.q: Roughly how large are the smallest structures that CaSSIS can still make out from Mars orbit?
a: A few metres, about the size of a lorry
A few millimetres, about the size of a grain of sand
A few kilometres, about the size of a small town
Hundreds of kilometres, about the size of Switzerland
101088.e: From a height of about 400 kilometres, CaSSIS reaches about 4.6 metres per image point. Boulders, dunes and gullies thus become visible.
101088.m: On Mars, CaSSIS can make out structures of a few metres.

101089.q: What are the stereo images from CaSSIS mainly used for scientifically?
a: For calculating digital height models of the surface
For measuring the temperature of Mars’s core
For determining the age of Mars in years
For transmitting data to the Earth
101089.e: From two images taken at different viewing angles, differences in height can be calculated. This produces three-dimensional terrain models of craters, slopes and gullies.
101089.m: Height models are calculated from stereo images.

101090.q: Why does CaSSIS photograph the surface of Mars through several colour filters?
a: To tell different rocks and ice apart
To protect the camera from dust
To save power during data transmission
101090.e: CaSSIS has four colour filters, from visible light to the near infrared. Rocks and ice reflect the colours differently and can be told apart in this way.
101090.m: Colour filters help to tell rocks and ice on Mars apart.

101091.q: What is the main aim of the orbiter that carries CaSSIS?
a: To detect trace gases such as methane in Mars’s atmosphere
To put a lander down on Phobos
To bring Martian rock to the Earth
To generate the magnetic field of Mars
101091.e: The Trace Gas Orbiter uses spectrometers to measure gases that occur only in very small amounts. Methane could point to geological or biological processes.
101091.m: The Trace Gas Orbiter searches for trace gases such as methane.

101092.q: On which rocket was Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024?
101092.e: The NASA probe was launched from the Kennedy Space Center on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. The Space Launch System had originally been planned.
101092.m: Europa Clipper was launched on a Falcon Heavy in 2024.

101093.q: Why does Europa Clipper fly past Europa many times rather than just once?
a: To cover different areas of the moon on each pass
Because the probe can switch its camera on only once per flight
Because otherwise Europa would fall onto Jupiter
101093.e: On its 49 flybys, the probe passes over different regions each time and so maps almost the whole moon. Between visits, it recovers far out from Jupiter’s radiation.
101093.m: Many flybys together make a map of the whole of Europa.

101094.q: Why does Europa Clipper orbit Jupiter and not the moon Europa directly?
a: To keep the radiation dose per flyby small
Because Europa has too little gravity
Because Europa is hidden by clouds
Because an orbit around Europa is forbidden
101094.e: Europa lies deep in Jupiter’s radiation belt. With short flybys followed by recovery phases far out, the electronics survive the radiation for longer.
101094.m: Short visits spare Europa Clipper too much radiation.

101095.q: When is Europa Clipper due to arrive at Jupiter?
101095.e: The probe uses swing-bys at Mars and the Earth and is due to reach Jupiter in April 2030. The scientific flybys of Europa begin in 2031.

101096.q: Roughly what span do Europa Clipper’s solar wings have?
101096.e: The solar wings measure about 30.5 metres from tip to tip. Europa Clipper is thus the largest probe NASA has ever built for a planetary mission.
101096.m: With a span of 30 metres, Europa Clipper is NASA’s largest planetary probe.

101097.q: What main question is Europa Clipper meant to answer about Jupiter’s moon Europa?
a: Whether Europa offers conditions friendly to life
Whether Europa is made of iron
Whether Europa will soon leave Jupiter
101097.e: A global salt-water ocean is suspected beneath the ice crust. The probe studies ice thickness, ocean, composition and geology, but does not search directly for living things.
101097.m: Europa Clipper checks whether Europa could be friendly to life.

101098.q: At which two planets does Europa Clipper pick up momentum on its way to Jupiter?
101098.e: Europa Clipper flew past Mars in March 2025 and is due to fly past the Earth in December 2026. Both swing-bys increase its speed towards Jupiter.
101098.m: Europa Clipper picks up momentum at Mars and the Earth.

101099.q: Which method does Europa Clipper’s instrument REASON use?
101099.e: REASON sends radar waves into the ice crust and receives the echoes from inner layers. In this way, ice thickness and possible pockets of water can be determined.
101099.m: REASON probes Europa’s ice with radar.

101100.q: What comes out in cryovolcanism instead of molten rock?
a: Volatile substances such as water, ammonia or methane
101100.e: Cryovolcanoes erupt so-called cryomagma, which is liquid at low temperatures. It consists mainly of water, often mixed with ammonia or methane.
101100.m: Ice volcanoes spit out water instead of lava.

101101.q: Where did Cassini discover fountains of water vapour and ice particles in 2005?
a: At the south pole of Enceladus
At the north pole of Titan
In the Cassini Division of the rings
101101.e: Fountains shoot into space from the so-called tiger stripes at Enceladus’s south pole. Their material also feeds Saturn’s E ring.
101101.m: Enceladus spits fountains of water into space at its south pole.

101102.q: Which space probe observed geysers on Neptune’s moon Triton in 1989?
101102.e: Voyager 2 saw dark plumes that rose to about 8 kilometres high. Probably heat from the Sun drives nitrogen gas through the ice crust.
101102.m: Voyager 2 discovered geysers on Triton in 1989.

101103.q: On which dwarf planet in the asteroid belt did the Dawn probe find an ice volcano?
101103.e: On Ceres, Dawn discovered Ahuna Mons, about 4 kilometres high. It probably consists of salty ice that has risen from the interior.
101103.m: Ceres also has an ice volcano.

101104.q: Which energy source mainly keeps cryovolcanism going on Enceladus?
101104.e: Enceladus runs on a slightly elliptical orbit. The changing tidal force deforms the moon and produces heat, which keeps the water beneath the ice liquid.
101104.m: Tidal forces heat Enceladus from the inside.

101105.q: Why can ammonia in water favour cryovolcanism?
a: It markedly lowers the freezing point
It makes the ice heavier than rock
It raises the melting point to over 100 °C
101105.e: A water-ammonia mixture stays liquid down to about minus 97 °C. In cold ice moons, liquid cryomagma can therefore form more easily.
101105.m: In an ice moon, ammonia acts like antifreeze.

101106.q: Why is Saturn’s moon Enceladus regarded as a possible place for extraterrestrial life?
a: Beneath its ice crust lies an ocean of liquid water
It has a dense oxygen atmosphere
It is the warmest moon in the Solar System
101106.e: The fountains at the south pole come from an ocean beneath the ice. In them, Cassini found salts, organic molecules and signs of hot springs on the sea floor.
101106.m: Beneath the ice of Enceladus lies an ocean.

101107.q: Which space probe found possible ice volcanoes on Pluto in 2015?
101107.e: On its flyby, New Horizons photographed two large mountains with depressions in the middle, Wright Mons and Piccard Mons. They count as possible ice volcanoes.
101107.m: New Horizons found possible ice volcanoes on Pluto.

101108.q: Which asteroid did the NASA probe DART hit on 26 September 2022?
101108.e: DART struck Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos. The double system posed no danger to the Earth and was suitable for the test.
101108.m: DART hit the asteroid moon Dimorphos.

101109.q: By roughly how much did DART’s impact shorten the orbital period of Dimorphos around Didymos?
101109.e: Before the impact, one orbit took about 11 hours and 55 minutes. The shortening was first put at 32 minutes and, after further measurements, at about 33 minutes. A change of at least 73 seconds had been expected.
101109.m: DART shortened the orbital period of Dimorphos by about half an hour.

101110.q: Which method of asteroid defence was tested with DART?
101110.e: A kinetic impactor passes momentum to the asteroid by a fast impact. DART hit at about 6 kilometres per second.
101110.m: DART tested defence by a targeted impact.

101111.q: Why was the change in Dimorphos’s orbit greater than expected from the probe’s impact alone?
a: Ejected material acted like an extra recoil
101111.e: On impact, large amounts of rock were thrown into space. Their recoil clearly strengthened the transfer of momentum.
101111.m: Debris thrown off strengthened the effect of DART.

101112.q: What was the DART probe carrying a small companion satellite for?
a: To photograph the impact from close by
To slow the probe down just before impact
To blow up the asteroid beforehand
To bring rock samples to the Earth
101112.e: The Italian small satellite LICIACube was released shortly before the impact and flew past Dimorphos a few minutes later. It supplied images of the ejecta cloud.
101112.m: A companion satellite photographed the impact of DART.

101113.q: Which ESA mission is to study the Didymos system closely after the DART impact?
101113.e: Hera was launched in October 2024 and is due to reach Didymos and Dimorphos at the end of 2026. It surveys the crater, mass and structure of Dimorphos.
101113.m: The ESA probe Hera inspects the consequences of the DART impact.

101114.q: How was the change in Dimorphos’s orbital period mainly measured?
a: With light curves from telescopes on the Earth
With a rope between the asteroids
With measurements of the Earth’s orbit
101114.e: When Dimorphos passes in front of or behind Didymos, the brightness of the system changes. From these eclipses, the orbital period can be determined precisely.
101114.m: Brightness curves revealed Dimorphos’s new orbital period.

101115.q: What does the abbreviation DART stand for?
101115.e: The name describes the aim: a double-asteroid system and the attempt to redirect an orbit. It was the first test of its kind.
101115.m: DART was the first test of deflecting an asteroid.

101116.q: Which asteroid did the Japanese probe Hayabusa2 study?
101116.e: Hayabusa2 reached the carbon-rich asteroid Ryugu in June 2018. Its predecessor Hayabusa had visited Itokawa.

101117.q: How did Hayabusa2 create an artificial crater on Ryugu?
a: With a copper projectile accelerated by an explosive charge
By the probe itself crashing into it
101117.e: On 5 April 2019, the Small Carry-on Impactor fired a copper projectile weighing about 2 kilograms at Ryugu. Afterwards, material from beneath the surface could be sampled.
101117.m: Hayabusa2 fired a copper projectile at Ryugu.

101118.q: Where did Hayabusa2’s sample capsule land in December 2020?
a: In the desert near Woomera in Australia
101118.e: The capsule landed on 6 December 2020 in the Woomera area of South Australia. It contained about 5 grams of material from Ryugu.
101118.m: Ryugu’s samples landed in Australia in 2020.

101119.q: What kind of vehicles did Hayabusa2 put down on Ryugu?
101119.e: Because of the tiny gravity, wheels hardly roll. The MINERVA-II rovers therefore moved by hopping.
101119.m: On Ryugu, the rovers hopped instead of driving.

101120.q: Which lander from DLR and CNES was put down on Ryugu by Hayabusa2?
101120.e: MASCOT landed on 3 October 2018 and worked for about 17 hours on battery power. It could turn and move itself using a swing arm.
101120.m: The German-French lander MASCOT explored Ryugu.

101121.q: What did researchers find in the Ryugu samples?
a: Amino acids and other organic compounds
101121.e: More than twenty amino acids and further organic molecules were detected in the samples. This supports the idea that asteroids brought building blocks of life to the Earth.
101121.m: Ryugu’s dust contains building blocks of life.

101122.q: What happened to the Hayabusa2 probe after it brought the Ryugu samples to the Earth in 2020?
a: It flew on to another asteroid
It burnt up together with the capsule
It landed in a museum in Japan
It stayed on Ryugu for ever
101122.e: Only the small sample capsule entered the Earth’s atmosphere. The probe itself still had propellant and set off on an extended mission to a tiny, fast-rotating asteroid, which it is due to reach in 2031.
101122.m: After returning the samples, Hayabusa2 flies on.

101123.q: How many times did Hayabusa2 briefly touch down on Ryugu to take samples?
101123.e: The first touch was on 22 February 2019 and the second on 11 July 2019 near the artificial crater. In this way, material from beneath the surface also got into the capsule.
101123.m: Hayabusa2 touched Ryugu twice for samples.

101124.q: What type of asteroid is Bennu, the target of OSIRIS-REx?
a: A stony asteroid made of basalt
101124.e: Bennu is a dark B-type asteroid with a lot of carbon. Such bodies count as almost unchanged material from the early days of the Solar System.
101124.m: Bennu is a dark, carbon-rich asteroid.

101125.q: Roughly how much material from the asteroid Bennu did OSIRIS-REx bring to the Earth in 2023?
101125.e: At about 121.6 grams, it is the largest asteroid sample ever brought back. The mission’s target had been at least 60 grams.
101125.m: OSIRIS-REx brought back over 120 grams of Bennu rock.

101126.q: How did OSIRIS-REx take the sample on Bennu?
a: With a puff of nitrogen that blew material into a collector head
With a grabbing arm that seized a boulder
With a harpoon and a net
