101126.e: In the touch-and-go, the sampling arm TAGSAM touched the surface for only a few seconds. A puff of nitrogen swirled dust and small stones into the collector head.
101126.m: OSIRIS-REx blew Bennu dust into its collector head.

101127.q: What emerged about Bennu’s surface when OSIRIS-REx touched down?
a: It is loose, like a ball pit
It is covered with liquid water
101127.e: The sampling arm sank in almost without resistance. Bennu is a rubble-pile asteroid made of loosely held-together chunks.
101127.m: Bennu is a loose pile of rubble.

101128.q: What is the space probe called after the sample return, and what is its target?
101128.e: After dropping off the capsule, the probe flew on. It is to explore Apophis shortly after its close pass of the Earth in April 2029.
101128.m: As OSIRIS-APEX, the probe visits the asteroid Apophis in 2029.

101129.q: Why is Bennu regarded as a potentially hazardous asteroid?
a: It has a small chance of hitting the Earth in the late 22nd century
It flies through the Earth’s atmosphere every year
It is the largest asteroid in the main belt
101129.e: Orbit calculations give an impact probability of about 1 in 2700 for the time around 2182. The data from OSIRIS-REx made the orbit known very precisely.
101129.m: Bennu could hit the Earth in the 22nd century with a small probability.

101130.q: What does the “REx” in the name OSIRIS-REx stand for?
101130.e: The full name is Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, Security, Regolith Explorer. Regolith is the loose debris on the surface.
101130.m: OSIRIS-REx was an explorer of asteroid regolith.

101131.q: What was found in the Bennu samples, among other things?
a: Water-bearing minerals and salts from evaporated brine
101131.e: The samples contain clay minerals, phosphates and evaporite salts. They show that liquid salt water once existed on Bennu’s parent body.
101131.m: Bennu’s rock tells of former salt water.

101132.q: Which international treaty of 1967 obliges states to avoid harmful contamination of celestial bodies?
101132.e: Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty requires states to avoid harmful contamination of other celestial bodies and adverse changes to the Earth’s environment.
101132.m: The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 is the basis of planetary protection.

101133.q: Why do less strict planetary-protection rules apply to a Moon landing than to a Mars landing?
a: On the Moon, life is practically ruled out
The Moon belongs to no state
The Moon is closer to the Earth
There is no gravity on the Moon
101133.e: The rules laid down by the international committee COSPAR depend on whether life would be possible on a celestial body. On the dry, airless Moon that is practically ruled out, on Mars it is not.
101133.m: The more likely life is, the stricter the planetary protection.

a: Carrying microbes from the Earth to other celestial bodies
Bringing extraterrestrial substances to the Earth
Polluting Earth orbit with space debris
101134.e: Microbes from the Earth could colonise alien environments or falsify the search for life. That is why probes are built in clean rooms and partly sterilised.
101134.m: Forward contamination brings Earth microbes into space.

101135.q: Why must rock samples from Mars first be kept securely sealed after arriving on the Earth?
a: They would crumble immediately in the air
101135.e: As long as it is not clear whether the samples contain life, they must not get into the Earth’s environment. Such missions fall into the strictest COSPAR category, V.
101135.m: Mars samples stay sealed until they are considered harmless.

101136.q: How were the Viking landers sterilised before their launch in 1975?
101136.e: The whole landers were dry-heated at about 111 °C for around 40 hours. Viking is still the benchmark for sterilisation today.
101136.m: The Viking landers were sterilised by heat.

101137.q: Why did NASA let the Galileo probe plunge into Jupiter in 2003?
a: Because it got too close to the Sun
101137.e: Galileo had supplied evidence of an ocean beneath Europa’s ice. An uncontrolled crash onto Europa could have contaminated this possible habitat.
101137.m: Galileo plunged into Jupiter so that Europa stayed clean.

a: The possible introduction of extraterrestrial organisms to the Earth
A rocket falling back onto the launch pad
The pollution of the Moon by exhaust gases
A probe’s return flight through the asteroid belt
101138.e: With sample returns, it must be ensured that no possible life forms get into the Earth’s biosphere. That is why Apollo astronauts were at first put in quarantine.
101138.m: Backward contamination concerns dangers to the Earth.

101139.q: What are “Special Regions” on Mars in the sense of planetary protection?
a: Areas in which microbes from the Earth could multiply
Landing sites with particularly flat terrain
Regions with a particularly strong magnetic field
Areas that belong to a state
101139.e: Where liquid water and suitable temperatures are possible at times, microbes from the Earth could grow. Probes for such areas have to meet stricter requirements.
101139.m: In Special Regions, Earth microbes could survive.

101140.q: What was concluded in 2015 from Cassini’s measurements of Enceladus’s slight wobble (libration)?
a: A global ocean lies beneath the ice crust
Enceladus has a solid iron core
Enceladus is made entirely of rock
101140.e: The wobble was too large for an ice shell fixed firmly to the core. The crust must therefore float on a continuous layer of water.
101140.m: Enceladus carries its ice crust on a global ocean.

101141.q: Roughly what launch speed relative to the Earth did New Horizons reach in 2006, a launch record?
101141.e: The Atlas V rocket with an extra stage accelerated the light probe to about 16.26 kilometres per second. It passed the Moon’s orbit after only about nine hours.
101141.m: New Horizons had the highest launch speed of any space probe so far.

101142.q: With which telescope was evidence of water-vapour plumes above Jupiter’s moon Europa found?
101142.e: In the ultraviolet range, Hubble observed hydrogen and oxygen emissions above Europa’s south pole, as well as plumes in front of Jupiter. The evidence has not yet been finally confirmed.
101142.m: Hubble supplied evidence of water fountains on Europa.

101143.q: Which life forms are typically counted when space probes are checked for cleanliness?
101143.e: Bacterial spores withstand dryness, cold and radiation particularly well. Their number on the surfaces is therefore used as a measure of biological cleanliness.
101143.m: The spore count shows how clean a space probe is.

101144.q: What is the difference between active and passive remote sensing systems?
a: Active systems send out radiation themselves and measure the echo
Active systems fly lower than passive ones
Passive systems work only at night
101144.e: Radar and lidar illuminate the surface themselves. Passive sensors such as optical cameras measure reflected sunlight or emitted heat.
101144.m: Active sensors bring their own illumination.

101145.q: Which two spectral ranges does the vegetation index NDVI use?
101145.e: Healthy leaf green strongly absorbs red light and very strongly reflects near infrared. The normalised difference between the two values shows how dense and healthy the vegetation is.
101145.m: The NDVI compares red with near infrared.

101146.q: Why do many Earth observation satellites fly in a sun-synchronous orbit?
a: They pass over each place at the same local time and so with similar lighting
They always stay above the same point on Earth
They are protected from all radiation there
They need no power supply there
101146.e: The orbital plane turns with the Sun once a year. This makes shadows and the Sun’s position comparable in repeated images.
101146.m: Sun-synchronous satellites always pass at the same local time.

101147.q: In which year was the first Landsat satellite launched, starting the longest image series in civilian Earth observation?
101147.e: Landsat 1 was launched in 1972. Since then the Landsat series has supplied images without interruption, showing changes in the land surface over decades.
101147.m: Landsat has been observing the Earth since 1972.

101148.q: What does the spectral resolution of a sensor describe?
a: The number and width of the measured wavelength ranges
The size of a pixel on the ground
The number of grey levels per channel
101148.e: Spatial resolution concerns pixel size, temporal resolution the repeat cycle and radiometric resolution the grey levels. Spectral resolution describes the channels.
101148.m: Spectral resolution tells you how finely a sensor separates colours.

101149.q: What characterises a hyperspectral sensor compared with a multispectral one?
a: It measures hundreds of narrow, seamlessly adjoining channels
It measures only a single broad channel
It works exclusively with radar waves
It always reaches a resolution below one centimetre
101149.e: Multispectral sensors usually have 4 to 15 broad channels. Hyperspectral data give an almost continuous spectrum for each pixel, which can be used, for example, to identify minerals.
101149.m: Hyperspectral sensors deliver a whole spectrum per pixel.

101150.q: Why can laser scanning (lidar) from an aircraft also capture the shape of the ground beneath a forest?
a: Some of the laser pulses pass through gaps in the canopy to the ground
Laser light passes completely through wood and leaves
The laser briefly melts the leaves away
Lidar measures the gravity of the ground
101150.e: Each pulse can produce several echoes. The last echoes often come from the ground, from which a digital terrain model without vegetation is calculated.
101150.m: Lidar sees through gaps in the leaves down to the forest floor.

101151.q: Which quantity can be determined with images in the thermal infrared?
101151.e: Every body emits heat radiation depending on its temperature. Thermal images therefore show, for example, urban heat islands or warm springs in bodies of water.
101151.m: Thermal images measure how warm a surface is.

101152.q: Which measured quantity does radar interferometry (InSAR) compare between two radar images?
a: The phase of the backscattered wave
The loudness of the echo in decibels alone
101152.e: If the distance between satellite and ground changes, the phase of the radar wave shifts. From this phase difference, deformations in the millimetre range can be determined.
101152.m: InSAR reads ground movements from phase differences.

101153.q: A radar satellite works with a wavelength of 5.6 cm. An interferogram shows 3 full colour cycles (fringes) over a slope. How large is the displacement in the satellite’s line of sight?
101153.e: One fringe corresponds to half the wavelength, because the path there and back counts, so 2.8 cm. Three fringes give 3 times 2.8 cm, which equals 8.4 cm.
101153.m: One fringe corresponds to half a radar wavelength.

101154.q: Why can a radar satellite also take measurements at night and through clouds?
a: It sends out its own microwaves, which pass through clouds
It measures the heat radiation of the clouds
It flies below the cloud cover
101154.e: Radar is an active method with its own illumination. Wavelengths of a few centimetres are hardly scattered by clouds.
101154.m: Radar sees at night and through clouds.

101155.q: What limitation does a single InSAR measurement have when recording movements?
a: It measures only the component in the satellite’s line of sight
It measures only movements over one metre
101155.e: Movements in a north to south direction are almost invisible to polar-orbiting satellites. Only combining ascending and descending orbits gives a more complete picture.
101155.m: InSAR sees only movements along its line of sight.

101156.q: What are ‘persistent scatterers’ in radar interferometry?
a: Points such as buildings or rocks that scatter back stably over a long time
Satellites that always stay in the same place
Clouds that permanently disturb the radar signal
101156.e: Such points give a consistent echo over years. This makes it possible to track slow subsidence of cities or slopes to the millimetre.
101156.m: Stable scatterers allow long-term measurements with InSAR.

101157.q: Why does InSAR often give unusable results in the Alps in winter?
a: Snow cover changes the backscatter, so coherence is lost
Radar does not work in the cold
The satellites do not fly over the Alps in winter
The days are too short for radar images
101157.e: Fresh snow, melting and drifting change the surface between two images. The phases then no longer match, which is called decorrelation.
101157.m: Snow destroys the coherence of radar images.

101158.q: Which mission in 2000 used radar interferometry to create an almost worldwide elevation model?
101158.e: The space shuttle Endeavour carried one antenna in its cargo bay and a second on a 60-metre mast. Both recorded at the same time, from which terrain heights were calculated.
101158.m: The SRTM mission measured the Earth’s heights in 2000.

101159.q: What does ‘synthetic aperture’ mean in SAR radar?
a: The satellite’s movement is used to imitate a very long antenna
The antenna is made of plastic
The radar image is artificially coloured
101159.e: During the flight, many echoes of the same point are recorded and processed together. This achieves a resolution like that of an antenna kilometres long.
101159.m: SAR replaces a huge antenna with the flight movement.

101160.q: With what accuracy can InSAR at best record slow ground movements over several years?
a: In the range of millimetres per year
In the range of metres per year
In the range of kilometres per year
Only to whole centimetres per decade
101160.e: With time series of many images, errors caused by the atmosphere can be removed. This makes subsidence rates of a few millimetres per year detectable.
101160.m: InSAR detects ground movements of millimetres per year.

101161.q: Who runs the Earth observation programme Copernicus?
a: The European Union together with ESA
101161.e: The EU finances and manages the programme. ESA is responsible for the Sentinel satellites, and EUMETSAT operates some of them.
101161.m: Copernicus is the EU’s Earth observation programme.

101162.q: What is the difference between the EU programme Copernicus and the EU programme Galileo?
a: Copernicus observes the Earth, Galileo is for navigation
Copernicus is for navigation, Galileo observes the Earth
Copernicus explores Mars, Galileo the Moon
101162.e: Copernicus supplies images and measurements of land, sea and atmosphere and was called GMES until 2012. Galileo is the European satellite navigation system, comparable to GPS.
101162.m: Copernicus observes the Earth, Galileo navigates.

101163.q: What kind of sensor do the Sentinel-1 satellites carry?
101163.e: Sentinel-1 delivers radar images regardless of the weather. They are used, for example, for sea ice, floods and ground movements with InSAR.
101163.m: Sentinel-1 observes the Earth with radar.

101164.q: What is the finest ground resolution reached by the multispectral images of Sentinel-2?
101164.e: Sentinel-2 measures in 13 spectral channels, the finest at 10 metres per pixel. That is enough to track fields, forest damage or glacier edges.
101164.m: Sentinel-2 sees the Earth with a resolution of up to 10 metres.

101165.q: What is the satellite Sentinel-5P with the instrument TROPOMI mainly responsible for?
a: Measuring trace gases such as nitrogen dioxide in the atmosphere
101165.e: TROPOMI is a spectrometer that covers the whole Earth every day. It measures nitrogen dioxide, ozone, methane and carbon monoxide, among other things.
101165.m: Sentinel-5P monitors air quality from space.

101166.q: What data policy applies to Copernicus Sentinel data?
a: They are freely available to everyone at no cost
They are available only to the military
They are available only for a licence fee
They are published only after 50 years
101166.e: The open data policy has led to heavy use in research, government and business. Anyone can download the data via online portals.
101166.m: Copernicus data are free of charge.

101167.q: What does the Copernicus Emergency Management Service do?
a: It quickly produces maps of disaster areas
It sends rescue teams into crisis areas
It predicts earthquakes to the minute
101167.e: After floods, fires or earthquakes, satellite images are turned into damage maps within hours. These help emergency services plan their work.
101167.m: The emergency service maps disasters from space.

101168.q: What is the main task of the satellite Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich?
a: To measure sea level with radar altimetry
To photograph clouds in visible light
To put out forest fires with lasers
To measure the Earth’s gravity field
101168.e: Sentinel-6 continues a series of global sea level measurements that has been running since 1992. The radar measures the height of the sea surface to within a few centimetres.
101168.m: Sentinel-6 measures the rise in sea level.

101169.q: How often can two Sentinel-2 satellites operating at the same time image the same place on the equator together?
101169.e: A single satellite needs 10 days for a complete cycle. With two satellites offset by 180 degrees, the repeat rate halves to 5 days, and at higher latitudes it is even shorter.
101169.m: Two Sentinel-2 satellites visit every place every 5 days.

101170.q: From which mountain in the Bregaglia did about 3 million cubic metres of rock fall in August 2017, triggering debris flows towards Bondo?
101170.e: The rockfall on Piz Cengalo killed eight hikers. Subsequent debris flows reached the village of Bondo, which had been evacuated in time thanks to monitoring and warnings.
101170.m: In 2017 a huge mass of rock fell from Piz Cengalo.

101171.q: What does an extensometer measure when monitoring a rock slope?
a: The change in distance across a crack
The air temperature in the rock
101171.e: A measuring wire or rod bridges a fissure. If the gap widens, the device shows the movement, often to a fraction of a millimetre.
101171.m: Extensometers show how far rock cracks are opening.

101172.q: Which measure had clearly slowed the landslide beneath the Grisons village of Brienz/Brinzauls by the end of 2025?
a: A drainage tunnel that lowers the water pressure in the slope
A large net over the whole slope
A concrete dam in the valley
101172.e: Water drains out of the slope through boreholes from the tunnel system, which is more than two kilometres long. Less pore water pressure relieves the sliding mass, and the movement fell from about 2.5 metres to a few centimetres per year.
101172.m: Drainage slows the landslide at Brienz/Brinzauls.

101173.q: What advantage does a ground-based radar have over satellite radar when monitoring an unstable slope?
a: It measures almost without interruption, about every few minutes
It also measures the type of rock
101173.e: Satellites pass over an area only every few days. A radar opposite the slope records movements continuously and can raise the alarm immediately if they speed up.
101173.m: Ground radar monitors a slope around the clock.

101174.q: Which measurement on a monitored rock slope suggests that a collapse is imminent?
a: The rock is moving faster and faster
The rock is moving evenly and slowly
The temperature in the valley falls
101174.e: Before a failure, the movement often speeds up sharply. From this acceleration, experts estimate when the rock might fall.
101174.m: Increasing speed warns of a rockfall.

101175.q: What are GNSS stations on a sliding slope used for?
a: They determine their position and so movements in three dimensions
They send warning sirens into the valley
101175.e: Satellite navigation such as GPS continuously provides the station’s coordinates to within millimetres or centimetres. This gives the direction and speed of the movement.
101175.m: GNSS stations track slope movements in three dimensions.

101176.q: Near which Valais village did about 30 million cubic metres of rock fall into the Matter Valley in two events in 1991?
101176.e: The Randa rockfalls in April and May 1991 buried the railway line and dammed the Vispa. Since then the rock face has been monitored scientifically.
101176.m: Randa experienced a massive rockfall in 1991.

101177.q: Why are measurements of unstable slopes often linked to threshold values?
a: To raise the alarm automatically or close roads when they are exceeded
101177.e: When speed or crack width reaches a set value, systems trigger warnings, traffic lights or closures. This way no time is lost on manual analysis.
101177.m: Threshold values turn measurements into rapid warnings.

101178.q: In which Valais valley is Blatten?
101178.e: Blatten is the village furthest up the Lötschental, a side valley on the north side of the Rhône Valley.
101178.m: Blatten lies at the far end of the Lötschental.

101179.q: What put extra load on the Birch Glacier before it broke off?
a: Rockfalls from the Kleines Nesthorn, whose debris stayed on the glacier
101179.e: From mid-May 2025, masses of rock repeatedly broke away from the Kleines Nesthorn. The debris weighed on the glacier, which then slid down the valley faster and faster.
101179.m: Rock debris from the Kleines Nesthorn overloaded the Birch Glacier.

101180.q: About how many people were evacuated from Blatten on 19 May 2025, nine days before the collapse?
101180.e: After a first partial evacuation on 17 May, the whole village with about 300 people was cleared. Monitoring thus prevented a much greater disaster.
101180.m: Thanks to timely evacuation, most people were safe.

101181.q: Which river was dammed by the debris masses at Blatten?
101181.e: The debris cone blocked the valley, and a lake formed behind it that flooded further houses. Villages further down were evacuated as a precaution.
101181.m: The dammed Lonza formed a lake behind the debris.

101182.q: Which technical term fits the 2025 event at Blatten best?
101182.e: A mixture of glacier ice and rock fell and flowed into the valley. In scientific literature the event is described as a rock-ice avalanche.
101182.m: At Blatten a rock-ice avalanche thundered into the valley.

101183.q: Which warning sign did experts observe on the Birch Glacier in the days before the collapse?
a: A sharply increasing flow speed of the glacier
A rise in air temperature to 40 °C
A sudden halt of all movement
Smoke coming out of the glacier
101183.e: Measurements showed an acceleration from a few metres to about 10 metres per day at the glacier front. Such acceleration is considered a typical sign of failure.
101183.m: A glacier flowing faster and faster announced the collapse.

101184.q: What did the canton do below Blatten at the end of May 2025 to reduce the danger from the dammed lake?
a: It had the gates of the Ferden reservoir opened
It blasted the debris cone away completely
It pumped the lake into a tunnel to Bern
101184.e: The Lonza had cut a path through the debris. The empty Ferden reservoir could thus take in water and sediment and pass them on.
101184.m: An opened reservoir helped to drain away the Lonza’s water.

101185.q: Which three types of dam typically hold back glacial lakes?
a: Moraines, glacier ice and rockfall material
101185.e: Moraine dams consist of loose debris, ice dams of the glacier itself. Each type of dam has its own ways of failing.
101185.m: Glacial lakes are dammed by moraines, ice or rock debris.

101186.q: Which glacial lake on the Plaine Morte suddenly drains towards Lenk in the Simmental in many summers?
101186.e: The ice-dammed lake drains through channels beneath the glacier. At the end of July 2018 this caused flooding in the valley, after which a channel was cut into the ice in 2019.
101186.m: Lac des Faverges on the Plaine Morte threatens Lenk when it bursts.

101187.q: Why does the outflow often increase faster and faster when an ice-dammed lake drains?
a: The flowing water melts the channels in the ice and widens them
The water makes the ice colder and harder
Rain fills the lake at the same time
The glacier actively pushes the lake out
101187.e: Frictional heat from the water melts the walls of the channels beneath the glacier. Larger channels let more water through, which speeds up the widening further.
101187.m: Outflowing water eats its way through the ice and gets faster.

101188.q: What often triggers the failure of a moraine dam?
a: An ice or rock avalanche that sends a flood wave over the dam
The lake freezing over in winter
101188.e: When material falls into the lake, a displacement wave forms. It washes over the loose dam and erodes it quickly, so the lake empties.
101188.m: Avalanches into glacial lakes can make moraine dams burst.

101189.q: Which Peruvian city was badly hit in 1941 by the outburst of Laguna Palcacocha?
101189.e: The lake’s moraine dam broke, and a flood wave of water and mud destroyed a large part of the city. Thousands of people died.
101189.m: The outburst of Laguna Palcacocha devastated Huaraz in 1941.

101190.q: What causes the glacial floods from Grímsvötn lake beneath the Vatnajökull in Iceland?
a: Volcanic heat melts ice into a subglacial lake that drains periodically
101190.e: An active volcano lies beneath the ice. When the water level rises high enough, the water lifts the ice barrier and drains suddenly.
101190.m: Volcanic heat fills a lake beneath the Vatnajökull that bursts periodically.

101191.q: Which ice-dammed lake on the Gorner Glacier used to drain towards Zermatt almost every summer?
101191.e: The marginal lake formed where the Gorner and Grenz glaciers meet and usually drained beneath the ice in summer. It was therefore studied intensively.
101191.m: The Gornersee regularly drained beneath the glacier.

101192.q: How was the danger from the Märjelensee on the Great Aletsch Glacier reduced at the end of the 19th century?
a: With a drainage tunnel towards the Fiesch Valley
With a wall of ice blocks
101192.e: The ice-dammed lake caused flooding in the Rhône Valley several times. A tunnel limited the water level and so the amount of water released in an outburst.
101192.m: A tunnel made the Märjelensee on the Aletsch Glacier safer.

101193.q: According to PERMOS estimates, roughly what share of Switzerland’s area has permafrost beneath it?
101193.e: Permafrost occurs mainly above about 2,500 metres, especially on north-facing slopes and scree. Its area is therefore larger than today’s glacier area.
101193.m: A small but significant part of Switzerland lies on permafrost.

101194.q: What is the top layer of soil above permafrost that thaws every summer called?
101194.e: The active layer freezes through again in winter. Its thickness is an important measurement because it increases as temperatures rise.
101194.m: The active layer thaws in summer and freezes in winter.

101195.q: What change has PERMOS been observing for years in many rock glaciers of the Swiss Alps?
a: They are turning into glaciers of pure ice
101195.e: Warmer ice inside is softer and deforms more easily, and there is also more meltwater. Many rock glaciers today move several times faster than in the 1990s.
101195.m: Warmer permafrost makes rock glaciers creep faster.

101196.q: Why do rockfalls from steep rock faces become more frequent when permafrost thaws?
a: Ice in cracks acts like glue and loses its holding power when it warms
The Sun blasts the rock directly
The snow pushes the rocks down
101196.e: In the hot summer of 2003 many rockfalls occurred, including on the Hörnli ridge of the Matterhorn. Bare ice was often visible at the break-off points.
101196.m: Thawing ice in cracks can make rock faces unstable.

101197.q: Why was a large protective dam built above Pontresina in the early 2000s?
a: To protect against avalanches and debris flows from the thawing permafrost on the Schafberg
As a dam for a power station
As part of a ski run
To protect against flooding from the Inn
101197.e: On the Schafberg, the permafrost in the debris is partly thawing, which makes debris flows more likely. The dam protects the village from avalanches and debris flows.
101197.m: Pontresina built a dam against dangers from the permafrost.

101198.q: What problems does thawing permafrost cause for cable car stations and huts in the high mountains?
101198.e: Many buildings in the high mountains stand on frozen ground. When the ice thaws, the ground loses its load-bearing capacity, and foundations have to be adapted or readjusted.
101198.m: Thawing permafrost endangers buildings in the high mountains.

101199.q: What are hollows and lakes called that form when ice-rich permafrost thaws and the ground sinks?
101199.e: Melting ground ice makes the volume shrink. In Siberia and Canada, numerous thermokarst lakes form in this way.
101199.m: Thermokarst forms when ice-rich ground thaws and sinks.

101200.q: Which huge depression in Siberia is the best-known example of rapidly advancing permafrost degradation?
101200.e: The Batagaika crater in Yakutia formed after deforestation and warming. It has been growing for decades because the exposed ground ice keeps thawing.
101200.m: The Batagaika crater shows how thawing permafrost changes the landscape.

101201.q: How do monitoring networks such as PERMOS measure the temperature of permafrost at depth?
a: With satellite images in visible light
With estimates from snow depths alone
101201.e: Chains of temperature sensors hang in boreholes down to depths of dozens of metres. This makes it possible to follow how warming slowly penetrates the ground.
101201.m: Boreholes reveal how warm the permafrost is at depth.

101202.q: How is lithium mainly extracted in the salt lakes of the Andes?
a: By evaporating brine in large ponds
101202.e: Lithium-rich brine is pumped from underground and evaporated in the sun for months. The lithium is then separated chemically.
101202.m: In the Andes, lithium-rich brine is left to evaporate.

101203.q: Which three countries form the so-called lithium triangle in South America?
101203.e: A large share of the world’s known lithium resources lies in the salt flats of these countries. Well-known examples are the Salar de Atacama and the Salar de Uyuni.
101203.m: Chile, Argentina and Bolivia form the lithium triangle.

101204.q: Which country was the world’s largest lithium producer in 2024?
101204.e: Australia mines lithium mainly from hard rock in pegmatites in open-pit mines. Bolivia has very large resources but produces little.
101204.m: Australia is the largest lithium producer (as of 2024).

101205.q: In which country is lithium mainly extracted from hard rock in open-pit mines rather than from salt lakes?
101205.e: Australia mines lithium-bearing minerals such as spodumene from pegmatites. Chile, Bolivia and Argentina extract lithium mainly from brine in salt flats.
101205.m: Australia gets lithium from rock, South America from salt lakes.

101206.q: Which environmental problem is particularly criticised in lithium mining in the salt flats of the Atacama?
a: The high water consumption in an extremely dry region
101206.e: Large amounts of water are lost during evaporation. Critics fear falling groundwater levels affecting lagoons, animals and indigenous communities.
101206.m: Lithium from salt flats costs a lot of water in deserts.

101207.q: From which source is lithium to be extracted in the Upper Rhine Graben?
a: From hot thermal water from geothermal plants
From river sand of the Rhine
101207.e: The deep water in the Upper Rhine Graben contains dissolved lithium. After the heat has been used, the lithium could be separated and the water pumped back.
101207.m: In the Upper Rhine Graben, lithium is to come from thermal water.

101208.q: Which mineral was discovered in Serbia’s Jadar Valley in 2004 and is important for a controversial lithium project?
101208.e: Jadarite is a lithium- and boron-bearing mineral known in large quantities only there. The mining project faces strong protests in Serbia.
101208.m: Jadarite was discovered in Serbia and contains lithium and boron.

101209.q: Why is lithium particularly well suited for high-performance batteries?
a: It is the lightest metal and has a very negative electrode potential
101209.e: The low mass and the high cell voltage give a high energy density. That is why lithium-ion batteries are found in mobile phones and electric cars.
101209.m: Light lithium stores a lot of energy per kilogram.

101210.q: In resource geology, what is the difference between a reserve and a resource?
a: A reserve can be mined economically with today’s technology and at today’s prices
A reserve always lies in the sea
A resource has already been mined
101210.e: Resources include all known or suspected deposits. Only the proven and economically recoverable part counts as a reserve.
101210.m: Reserves are the economically mineable part of resources.

101211.q: What does the cut-off grade of a deposit refer to?
a: The minimum content at which rock is considered worth mining
The maximum depth of a mine
The price of the raw material on the stock exchange
101211.e: Rock below the cut-off grade is treated as waste rock. If the commodity price rises, the cut-off grade can fall and the reserve can grow.
101211.m: The cut-off grade separates ore from waste rock.

101212.q: When did most banded iron formations, today’s most important iron ore deposits, form?
a: Mainly in the Precambrian, more than 1.8 billion years ago
In the Tertiary, 30 million years ago
101212.e: Dissolved iron in the sea was precipitated as oxygen from photosynthesis increased. This created layers of iron oxides alternating with siliceous rock.
101212.m: Banded iron formations tell of the rise of oxygen in early Earth history.

101213.q: From which basin in South Africa does about 40 per cent of all the gold ever mined on Earth come?
101213.e: The gold there lies in conglomerates about three billion years old, which are thought to be fossil river deposits. The mines reach down almost 4 kilometres.
101213.m: The Witwatersrand Basin is the richest gold deposit on Earth.

101214.q: How do the Swiss salt works extract rock salt from underground?
a: By solution mining, dissolving it with water and pumping up the brine
By blasting and carrying it away on conveyor belts
101214.e: Water is pressed into boreholes and dissolves the salt of the Triassic layers. The brine is pumped up and evaporated in salt works, for example in Riburg, Schweizerhalle and Bex.
101214.m: Swiss salt comes from underground as brine.

101215.q: In which rock are primary diamonds mainly found?
101215.e: Kimberlite pipes quickly carry material from depths of more than 150 kilometres to the surface. Only there are the pressures high enough for diamond to be stable.
101215.m: Diamonds come in kimberlite from the Earth’s mantle.

101216.q: Which country has by far mined the most rare earths in recent years?
101216.e: China recently supplied about two thirds of world production. The Bayan Obo deposit in Inner Mongolia is the largest known.
101216.m: China dominates the mining of rare earths.

101217.q: From which geological complex in South Africa does most of the world’s mined platinum come?
101217.e: In the Bushveld Complex, platinum metals and chromite became concentrated in layers of a huge magmatic intrusion. It holds the largest known platinum deposits.
101217.m: The Bushveld Complex supplies most of the world’s platinum.

101218.q: What does the abbreviation Nagra stand for?
a: National Cooperative for the Disposal of Radioactive Waste
National Agency for Geology and Raw Material Analysis
101218.e: Nagra was founded in 1972 by the operators of the nuclear power stations and the Confederation. It is based in Wettingen in the canton of Aargau.
101218.m: Nagra plans the disposal of radioactive waste in Switzerland.

101219.q: Which site did Nagra propose for the deep geological repository in September 2022?
101219.e: Nördlich Lägern lies in the cantons of Zurich and Aargau near the border with Germany. Nagra described it as the site with the largest safety margins.
101219.m: Nagra wants to build the deep repository at Nördlich Lägern.

101220.q: When did Nagra submit the general licence applications for the deep repository to the Confederation?
101220.e: The applications for the deep repository and for a fuel assembly packaging plant reached the Swiss Federal Office of Energy on 19 November 2024.
101220.m: Nagra submitted its applications in November 2024.

101221.q: What does the term ‘combined repository’ mean at Nagra?
a: A repository for high-level as well as low- and intermediate-level waste at the same site
A repository for nuclear waste and household rubbish
A repository that is also a power station
101221.e: Instead of two separate deep repositories, both categories of waste are to be stored in one place, but in separate parts of the repository.
101221.m: In a combined repository, all types of radioactive waste lie in the same place.

101222.q: Where is the fuel assembly packaging plant to be built, in which spent fuel assemblies are placed in disposal containers?
a: At the interim storage facility in Würenlingen
At the Gösgen nuclear power station
In the Mont Terri rock laboratory
101222.e: The plant is to be built at the existing central interim storage facility Zwilag in the canton of Aargau. The waste is already stored there today.
101222.m: The packaging plant is planned in Würenlingen.

101223.q: Which three siting regions did Nagra investigate in depth in the last stage of the sectoral plan?
a: Jura Ost, Nördlich Lägern and Zürich Nordost
Mont Terri, Napf and Jura Süd
Bern Nord, Basel Ost and Genf Süd
101223.e: All three regions lie in northern Switzerland, where Opalinus Clay occurs at a suitable depth. They were compared using boreholes and seismic surveys.
101223.m: Jura Ost, Nördlich Lägern and Zürich Nordost were the last candidates.

101224.q: In which rock laboratory in the Bernese Oberland has Nagra been researching questions of deep disposal in granite since 1984?
101224.e: The Grimsel rock laboratory lies in crystalline rock. There, for example, the transport of substances in fissures and the behaviour of barriers are tested.
101224.m: In the Grimsel rock laboratory, Nagra does research in granite.

101225.q: What political right do Swiss voters have in the decision on the general licence for the deep repository?
a: They can call an optional referendum
They must vote in a mandatory referendum in any case
Only the host canton may vote
101225.e: The Federal Council grants the general licence, and Parliament must approve it. A referendum can be called against this decision, and a vote would be possible around 2031.
101225.m: The people can vote on the deep repository by referendum.

101227.q: Roughly how old is Opalinus Clay?
101227.e: Opalinus Clay was deposited in the Lower Jurassic as fine mud in a shallow sea. It is therefore older than the folding of the Alps.
101227.m: Opalinus Clay is about 174 million years old.

101228.q: Which property makes Opalinus Clay particularly suitable as host rock for a deep repository?
a: It is very impermeable to water
It is very hard and brittle like granite
It contains a lot of crude oil
101228.e: Water hardly moves in Opalinus Clay, and dissolved substances travel almost only by diffusion. This holds back radionuclides for a very long time.
101228.m: Opalinus Clay lets almost no water through.

101229.q: What is meant by ‘self-sealing’ in Opalinus Clay?
a: Cracks close because clay minerals swell
The clay forms a crust of glass
Heat turns the rock into concrete
101229.e: When water enters fissures, the clay minerals swell and close the pathways again. So the rock hardly loses its tightness even after disturbances.
101229.m: Swelling clay minerals seal cracks in Opalinus Clay by themselves.

101230.q: In which canton is the Mont Terri rock laboratory, where Opalinus Clay has been studied since 1996?
101230.e: The laboratory is near St-Ursanne and is run by swisstopo. More than 20 partners from about ten countries carry out research there in about 1,200 metres of tunnels.
101230.m: In the canton of Jura, the Mont Terri rock laboratory studies Opalinus Clay.

101231.q: Roughly how thick is the layer of Opalinus Clay in the Nördlich Lägern area?
101231.e: The layer there is about 100 metres thick and lies several hundred metres deep. The repository is to be built in the middle of this layer.
101231.m: Opalinus Clay is about 100 metres thick at Nördlich Lägern.

101232.q: Why do the clay minerals in Opalinus Clay additionally hold back many radioactive substances?
a: Positively charged ions attach to their surfaces (sorption)
The clay minerals destroy the radioactivity
The clay minerals evaporate the water
101232.e: Clay minerals have negatively charged surfaces. Many radionuclides are bound there and so travel even more slowly than the water.
101232.m: Clay minerals bind many radionuclides to their surfaces.

101233.q: What difficulty does Opalinus Clay cause when building tunnels?
a: It can swell and deform, which puts strain on the lining
It is so hard that drills break
101233.e: On contact with water and through unloading during excavation, the clay can swell and press on the tunnel lining. This must be taken into account in construction and maintenance.
101233.m: Opalinus Clay can swell and press in tunnel construction.

101234.q: Why is earthquake early warning possible at all?
a: The faster P waves and radio signals travel ahead of the destructive S waves and surface waves
Earthquakes announce themselves days in advance through animal noises
The Earth sends a radio signal before every earthquake
101234.e: Seismometers near the source detect the first waves and send a warning at the speed of light. Places further away gain a few seconds this way.
101234.m: Earthquake warnings use the head start of the P waves.

101235.q: A place is 70 km from the earthquake source. The P wave travels at 6 km/s, the S wave at 3.5 km/s. About how many seconds after the P wave does the S wave arrive?
101235.e: The P wave needs 70 divided by 6, so about 11.7 s, the S wave 70 divided by 3.5, so 20 s. The difference is about 8.3 s.
101235.m: The gap between P and S waves grows with distance.

101236.q: What is the ‘blind zone’ of an earthquake early warning system?
a: The area near the epicentre where the warning comes too late
An area without mobile phone coverage
An area where earthquakes never happen
101236.e: Measuring, analysing and raising the alarm take a few seconds. Close to the source, the strong waves have already arrived by then.
101236.m: Near the epicentre every earthquake warning comes too late.

101237.q: When does the annual siren test normally take place in Switzerland?
a: On the first Wednesday in February
On the first Monday in June
On the last Friday in December
101237.e: The test checks the general alarm and, in areas below dams, also the water alarm. The public does not need to do anything.
101237.m: The siren test is on the first Wednesday in February.

101238.q: Which mountain torrent in Valais does the WSL use as a test site for a debris flow warning system with geophones and radar?
101238.e: The Illgraben near Leuk produces several debris flows almost every year. Sensors detect them early and trigger warnings at bridges and paths.
101238.m: At the Illgraben, debris flows are detected and reported automatically.

101239.q: According to the United Nations, which four elements make up an effective early warning system?
a: Risk knowledge, monitoring, spreading the warning and the ability to respond
Police, fire brigade, army and hospitals
101239.e: A measuring network alone is not enough. The warning must reach people, and they must know how to react.
101239.m: Early warning needs knowledge, measurement, communication and preparation.

101240.q: Which international UN framework applies from 2015 to 2030 for reducing disaster risk?
101240.e: The framework adopted in the Japanese city of Sendai sets seven global targets, including more access to early warning systems.
101240.m: The Sendai Framework aims to reduce disaster risk by 2030.

101241.q: How do tsunami warning systems in the deep sea detect a passing wave?
a: With pressure sensors on the seabed that send data via buoys
With thermometers on the water surface
101241.e: A tsunami lifts the whole column of water, which can be measured on the seabed as a small change in pressure. A buoy relays the values via satellite to warning centres.
101241.m: Pressure sensors on the seabed detect tsunamis on the open sea.

101242.q: Which quantity is plotted on the x-axis of a mass spectrum?
101242.e: A mass spectrometer separates ions by their ratio of mass to charge. For singly charged ions, m/z equals the ion mass directly.
101242.m: A mass spectrometer sorts ions by their mass-to-charge ratio.

101243.q: What happens to the molecules in a mass spectrometer before they are sorted by mass?
101243.e: Only charged particles can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields. That is why the molecules are ionised first.
101243.m: In a mass spectrometer, molecules are first turned into ions.

101244.q: A mass spectrum shows two molecular ion peaks 2 units apart with an intensity ratio of about 3 to 1. Which element does the compound probably contain?
101244.e: Chlorine consists of about 76 per cent ³⁵Cl and about 24 per cent ³⁷Cl. This gives the typical ratio of about 3 to 1 between M and M+2.
101244.m: An M+2 peak a third the height of the molecular ion peak points to a chlorine atom.

101245.q: Which isotope pattern does the molecular ion of a compound with exactly one bromine atom show?
a: M and M+2 about equally high
M+2 about a third of M
M+1 about half as high as M
Only a single peak at M
101245.e: Bromine occurs as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in almost equal proportions. That is why M and M+2 appear almost equally strong.
101245.m: With bromine, the M and M+2 peaks are almost equally high.

101246.q: Why do molecules often break into several fragments during electron impact ionisation?
a: The colliding electrons transfer a lot of energy
The magnetic field tears them apart
They react with oxygen from the air
101246.e: Fast electrons knock an electron out of the molecule and also give off energy. The ion therefore often breaks into typical fragments that act like a fingerprint.
101246.m: High-energy electrons break molecules into typical fragments.

101247.q: Why do proteins need particularly gentle ionisation in a mass spectrometer?
a: Otherwise the large molecules break into many fragments
101247.e: Large biomolecules are delicate and break apart with harsh methods. Gentle techniques such as electrospray ionisation bring them into the instrument intact.
101247.m: Large biomolecules must be ionised gently so that they stay whole.

101248.q: In a time-of-flight mass spectrometer (TOF), which ions with the same charge reach the detector first?
a: The ions with the greatest polarity
All ions at the same time
101248.e: All ions get the same kinetic energy, so light ions fly faster. The flight time can therefore be used to calculate m/z.
101248.m: In a time-of-flight analyser, light ions arrive before heavy ones.

101249.q: What did the first mass spectrographs around 1920 show about many chemical elements?
a: Their atoms all weigh the same
101249.e: With the mass spectrograph, atoms of different masses were found in many non-radioactive elements. This also explained atomic masses that are not whole numbers.
101249.m: Mass spectrometry revealed the isotopes of many elements.

101250.q: At which m/z value would you expect the molecular ion peak of ethanol C₂H₆O (C 12, H 1, O 16)?
101250.e: 2 · 12 + 6 · 1 + 16 = 46. For the singly charged molecular ion, m/z equals the molecular mass.
101250.m: The molecular ion peak shows the mass of the whole molecule.

101251.q: Which property of certain atomic nuclei does NMR spectroscopy use?
101251.e: Nuclei with nuclear spin, such as the hydrogen nucleus, have a magnetic moment. In a strong magnetic field they absorb radio waves of a particular frequency.
101251.m: NMR uses the magnetism of atomic nuclei.

101252.q: What does the abbreviation NMR stand for?
101252.e: NMR stands for “nuclear magnetic resonance”. It is also called nuclear spin resonance.

101253.q: How many groups of different hydrogen atoms does ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) show in the ¹H NMR spectrum?
101253.e: The H atoms of the CH₃ group, the CH₂ group and the OH group each have a different chemical environment. Each group gives its own signal.
101253.m: Hydrogen atoms in the same environment give the same NMR signal.

101254.q: What does the integral of a signal in the ¹H NMR spectrum tell you?
101254.e: The area under a signal is proportional to the number of hydrogen nuclei producing it. This lets you work out the ratio of the different groups of protons.
101254.m: The signal area in the proton spectrum shows how many hydrogen atoms are involved.

101255.q: What does it mean when two hydrogen atoms appear in different places in the NMR spectrum?
a: They have a different chemical environment
101255.e: Neighbouring atoms and bonds shield each nucleus from the magnetic field to a different degree. That is why the signals appear at different chemical shifts.
101255.m: The position of an NMR signal reveals the atom's environment.

101256.q: Which Zurich-born physicist shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics with Edward Purcell for developing nuclear magnetic resonance?
101256.e: Felix Bloch was born in Zurich in 1905 and studied at ETH. He and Purcell independently developed methods for measuring nuclear magnetic resonance in solids and liquids.
101256.m: Felix Bloch from Zurich is one of the founders of nuclear magnetic resonance.

101257.q: Why are samples for ¹H NMR usually dissolved in deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃?
a: So that the solvent does not produce a large proton signal
So that the sample evaporates faster
So that the sample does not oxidise
So that the molecular mass increases
101257.e: Deuterium has a completely different resonance frequency from ¹H and does not appear in the proton spectrum. The instrument also uses the deuterium signal to stabilise the magnetic field.
101257.m: Deuterated solvents stop the solvent from covering up the proton spectrum.

101258.q: Which medical imaging method is based on the same physical principle as NMR spectroscopy?
101258.e: Magnetic resonance imaging measures the nuclear magnetic resonance of hydrogen nuclei in the body. Field gradients link the signal to a location.
101258.m: Magnetic resonance imaging is nuclear magnetic resonance applied to people.

101259.q: What advantage does an NMR spectrometer with a stronger magnetic field bring, for example 800 MHz instead of 300 MHz?
a: A shorter half-life of the sample
Measurement without nuclei that have spin
101259.e: With a stronger field, the frequency gaps between signals and the population difference of the spin states increase. Signals overlap less and are stronger.
101259.m: A stronger magnetic field makes NMR spectra sharper and more sensitive.

101260.q: What did Richard R. Ernst receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1991?
a: For contributions to high-resolution NMR spectroscopy
101260.e: Ernst developed Fourier transform NMR and multidimensional NMR spectroscopy. He received the prize alone.
101260.m: Richard Ernst was honoured in 1991 for modern NMR spectroscopy.

101261.q: In which Swiss city was Richard R. Ernst born in 1933?
101261.e: Ernst came from Winterthur and also died there in 2021. He studied and did research at ETH Zurich.
101261.m: The Nobel Prize winner Richard Ernst was born in Winterthur.

101262.q: At which university was Richard R. Ernst a professor for most of his career?
101262.e: Ernst did his doctorate at ETH Zurich and returned there as a researcher in 1968. He later became professor of physical chemistry there.
101262.m: Richard Ernst taught and did research at ETH Zurich.

101263.q: Which mathematical method did Ernst use to obtain a whole NMR spectrum from a short radio frequency pulse?
101263.e: Ernst excited all the nuclei at once with a pulse and broke the fading signal down into its frequencies with the Fourier transform. This made measurements much faster and more sensitive.
101263.m: The Fourier transform turns the NMR time signal into a spectrum.

101264.q: Which medical imaging method, like Richard Ernst's NMR spectroscopy, is based on nuclear magnetic resonance?
101264.e: MRI uses the same principle as NMR: atomic nuclei in a magnetic field send out radio signals. Ernst's methods also contributed to the development of MRI.
101264.m: MRI and NMR are based on nuclear magnetic resonance.

101265.q: What do chemists mainly use NMR spectroscopy for?
a: To work out the structure of molecules
101265.e: NMR shows how the atoms in a molecule are connected. It is one of the most important methods for working out structures.
101265.m: NMR tells you how a molecule is built.

101266.q: Which works of art did Richard R. Ernst collect and study with spectroscopic methods?
101266.e: Ernst was a great collector of Tibetan thangka paintings. He used Raman spectroscopy to analyse the pigments used.
101266.m: Richard Ernst studied the colours of Tibetan scroll paintings with spectroscopy.

101267.q: What does an NMR instrument need to align the atomic nuclei of a sample?
101267.e: Atomic nuclei with nuclear spin behave like tiny magnets and line up in a magnetic field. A radio pulse disturbs this alignment, and the nuclei send out measurable signals.
101267.m: NMR instruments work with strong magnetic fields.

101268.q: What did Kurt Wüthrich receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 2002?
a: For determining the structure of biomolecules in solution by NMR
101268.e: Wüthrich showed how to use NMR to determine the three-dimensional structure of proteins in solution. The other half of the prize went to Fenn and Tanaka for mass spectrometry.
101268.m: Kurt Wüthrich was the first to determine protein structures in solution with NMR.

101269.q: Which canton does the chemistry Nobel Prize winner Kurt Wüthrich come from?
101269.e: Wüthrich was born in 1938 in Aarberg in the Bernese Seeland and studied at the University of Bern. He later did research at ETH Zurich.
101269.m: Kurt Wüthrich comes from the canton of Bern.

101270.q: What advantage does determining protein structures by NMR have over X-ray crystallography?
a: The protein does not have to be crystallised
It only works with large proteins
It always gives the molecular mass
101270.e: Many proteins are hard to crystallise. With NMR they are measured in solution, closer to their natural environment.
101270.m: With NMR you study proteins in solution, without any crystal.

101271.q: Which particles in the protein mainly provide the measured signals in Wüthrich's NMR method?
101271.e: In nuclear magnetic resonance, atomic nuclei in a strong magnetic field respond to radio waves. Proteins contain a great many hydrogen atoms, whose nuclei are easy to measure.
101271.m: Protein NMR mainly measures the signals of hydrogen nuclei.

101272.q: At which university did Kurt Wüthrich teach as professor of biophysics?
101272.e: Wüthrich did research at ETH Zurich from the late 1960s and became professor of biophysics there. He also did research at the Scripps Research Institute in California.
101272.m: Kurt Wüthrich did research as a biophysicist at ETH Zurich.

101273.q: Besides Switzerland, in which country did Kurt Wüthrich also do research as a professor?
101273.e: From 2001, Wüthrich also held a professorship at the Scripps Research Institute in California. He travelled back and forth between Zurich and the USA.
101273.m: Kurt Wüthrich did research in Zurich and in California.

101274.q: In 1996, Wüthrich's group used NMR to determine the structure of which protein linked to the disease BSE?
101274.e: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause diseases such as BSE. Wüthrich's group determined the structure of the normal prion protein of the mouse.
101274.m: In 1996, Wüthrich's group worked out the structure of the prion protein with NMR.

101275.q: Why is it so important to know the three-dimensional structure of a protein?
a: The shape determines how the protein works
The shape determines the blood group
The shape determines the age of the cell
The shape determines the colour of the protein
101275.e: Enzymes, receptors and antibodies only work if their shape fits exactly. Knowing the structure helps, for example, to develop medicines in a more targeted way.

101276.q: For which method did Jacques Dubochet from Vaud receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017?
101276.e: Dubochet shared the prize with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson. Cryo-electron microscopy makes it possible to image frozen biomolecules in their natural shape.
101276.m: Jacques Dubochet received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for cryo-electron microscopy.

101277.q: Which canton does the chemistry Nobel Prize winner Jacques Dubochet come from?
101277.e: Dubochet was born in 1942 in Aigle in the canton of Vaud. He later became a professor at the University of Lausanne.
101277.m: Jacques Dubochet is from Vaud and did his research in Lausanne.

101278.q: At which university was Jacques Dubochet a professor from 1987?
101278.e: After his time in Heidelberg, Dubochet moved to the University of Lausanne. There he headed the Laboratory for Ultrastructural Analysis.
101278.m: Jacques Dubochet taught at the University of Lausanne.

101279.q: What was Dubochet's crucial contribution to cryo-electron microscopy?
a: Freezing water so fast that it sets like glass
101279.e: When frozen in a flash, water does not form a crystal lattice but amorphous, glassy ice. In this way, biomolecules keep their natural shape.
101279.m: Dubochet vitrified water so that biomolecules stay undamaged when frozen.

101280.q: Why are normal ice crystals a problem in samples for electron microscopy?
a: They scatter the electron beam and destroy structures
101280.e: Ice crystals strongly diffract the electrons and cover up the image of the molecules. As they grow, they can also deform delicate structures.
101280.m: Ice crystals spoil the electron microscope image and damage biomolecules.

101281.q: Which coolant is used to keep samples very cold during measurement in cryo-electron microscopy?
101281.e: Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 °C. This keeps the glassy ice of the sample stable so that it does not crystallise.
101281.m: In cryo-electron microscopy, samples are cooled with liquid nitrogen.

101282.q: What does the term “vitrification”, which Dubochet used for his freezing method, mean?
101282.e: The Latin word “vitrum” means glass. In vitrification, water sets so quickly that it becomes solid and glassy without crystals.
101282.m: Vitrification means turning into glass: water sets without ice crystals.

101283.q: Why do biological samples dry out in an ordinary electron microscope?
a: Because there is a vacuum in the microscope
Because the electron beam breaks water down chemically
Because the microscope is strongly heated
Because the sample is stained first
101283.e: Electrons need a high vacuum, otherwise they collide with air molecules. In a vacuum, liquid water evaporates immediately, whereas frozen water is kept.
101283.m: In the vacuum of an electron microscope, liquid water would evaporate immediately.

101284.q: Which gas is often used as the carrier gas in gas chromatography?
101284.e: The carrier gas must be unreactive and carry the sample through the column. Helium, hydrogen or nitrogen are common.
101284.m: An inert carrier gas such as helium forms the mobile phase in gas chromatography.

101285.q: Which property must substances have so that they can be analysed directly by gas chromatography?
a: They can be vaporised without breaking down
101285.e: The sample is vaporised in the injector and must travel through the column as a gas. Substances that break down in the process are unsuitable or must be converted first.
101285.m: For gas chromatography, substances must vaporise without breaking down.

101286.q: In gas chromatography, which measured value is used to identify a substance under fixed conditions?
101286.e: The retention time is the time from injection until the signal appears at the detector. Under the same conditions it is characteristic of a substance.
101286.m: The retention time is a substance's fingerprint in gas chromatography.

101287.q: What does a gas chromatograph produce at the end of a measurement?
a: a chromatogram with one signal for each separated substance
an X-ray image of the sample
101287.e: The detector at the end of the column registers each substance that arrives there. This produces a diagram in which each substance appears as its own peak.
101287.m: In the chromatogram, each separated substance appears as its own peak.

101288.q: Why is the oven temperature raised during many gas chromatography measurements?
a: So that substances that are hard to vaporise also leave the column quickly
So that the carrier gas becomes heavier
So that the detector cools down
So that the column gets longer
101288.e: At a low temperature, easily vaporised substances are separated well. Heating then lets the less volatile substances leave the column in a reasonable time.
101288.m: A temperature programme separates volatile and less volatile substances in one run.

101289.q: On what principle does chromatography separate a mixture?
a: The substances are distributed differently between the mobile and stationary phases.
The substances are sorted by their radioactivity.
The substances are deflected in a magnetic field.
The substances are filtered by their colour.
101289.e: A substance that sticks strongly to the stationary phase moves slowly. A substance that prefers to stay in the mobile phase moves quickly. This separates the substances.
101289.m: Chromatography separates substances by how they are distributed between two phases.

101290.q: Other things being equal, which substance usually leaves the column of a gas chromatograph first?
a: the substance with the lowest boiling point
the substance with the highest boiling point
the substance with the greatest molecular mass
the substance with the strongest colour
101290.e: Volatile substances stay almost entirely in the carrier gas and are carried quickly through the column. Less volatile substances spend longer in the stationary phase.
101290.m: Volatile substances appear first in gas chromatography.

101291.q: What is the long, thin tube called in which the substances are separated in gas chromatography?
101291.e: The column is often many metres long and coiled up. It sits in an oven, and the carrier gas carries the sample through it.
101291.m: The separation takes place in a long, thin column.

101292.q: Which combination of two methods separates mixtures and at the same time identifies the components from their fragments?
101292.e: Gas chromatography separates the mixture and the attached mass spectrometer gives a spectrum for each substance. GC-MS is standard in environmental, doping and food analysis.
101292.m: Combining gas chromatography and mass spectrometry separates and identifies at the same time.

101293.q: What is the aim of green chemistry?
a: designing chemical processes with as little waste and danger as possible
carrying out all reactions at room temperature
101293.e: Green chemistry aims to avoid waste, toxic substances and energy use right from the planning of a synthesis. Paul Anastas and John Warner summed this up in twelve principles in 1998.
101293.m: Green chemistry avoids waste and danger right from the planning stage.

101294.q: Which type of reaction basically has an atom economy of 100 per cent?
101294.e: In an addition, all the atoms of the reactants are built into a single product. No by-products form.
101294.m: Addition reactions build all the atoms of the starting materials into the product.

101295.q: What is the atom economy of the reaction CH₃Br + NaOH to CH₃OH + NaBr, using M(CH₃Br) = 94.9 g/mol, M(NaOH) = 40.0 g/mol and M(CH₃OH) = 32.0 g/mol?
101295.e: Atom economy is the molar mass of the desired product divided by the sum of the reactant molar masses. 32.0 / (94.9 + 40.0) = 32.0 / 134.9 gives about 0.24.
101295.m: Atom economy compares the mass of the target product with the mass of all the starting materials.

101296.q: The E-factor is the mass of waste divided by the mass of product. A synthesis produces 2 kg of product and 50 kg of waste. What is the E-factor?
101296.e: 50 kg of waste divided by 2 kg of product gives 25. So 25 kg of waste is produced for every kilogram of product.
101296.m: The smaller the E-factor, the less waste per kilogram of product.

101298.q: Which supercritical fluid is used as an environmentally friendly solvent, for example to decaffeinate coffee?
101298.e: Supercritical CO₂ is non-toxic, non-flammable and easy to remove as a gas after extraction. In this way it replaces organic solvents.
101298.m: Supercritical carbon dioxide is a green solvent with no toxic residues.

101299.q: Why does green chemistry prefer catalysts to stoichiometric reagents?
a: Catalysts are not used up and save waste
Catalysts always raise the yield to 100 per cent
101299.e: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. Stoichiometric reagents, by contrast, usually end up as waste.
101299.m: Catalysts save raw materials because they are not used up in the reaction.

101300.q: Why are syntheses with fewer reaction steps considered more environmentally friendly?
a: They need less energy and solvent and produce less waste.
They always give more colourful products.
They need no starting materials at all.
101300.e: Every step needs solvents, energy and purification, and some product is lost. Fewer steps therefore save raw materials and avoid waste.
101300.m: Fewer synthesis steps mean less waste.

101301.q: Why are PFAS often called “forever chemicals”?
a: Because the carbon-fluorine bond is extremely stable
Because they break down immediately in water
Because they only occur in space
101301.e: The C-F bond is one of the strongest single bonds in organic chemistry. That is why PFAS are practically not broken down in the environment.
101301.m: Because of the strong carbon-fluorine bond, PFAS stay in the environment almost for ever.

101302.q: What does “perfluorinated” mean for an alkyl chain?
a: All the hydrogen atoms on the carbon are replaced by fluorine
The chain contains exactly one fluorine atom
The chain is closed into a ring
The chain contains fluorine and chlorine
101302.e: The prefix “per” means completely. In a perfluorinated chain, every carbon atom carries only fluorine instead of hydrogen.
101302.m: In a perfluorinated chain, every hydrogen on the carbon is replaced by fluorine.

101303.q: Which two properties make PFAS so popular for coating textiles and paper?
a: They conduct electricity and are magnetic
101303.e: PFAS chains are both hydrophobic and lipophobic. That is why they were used for outdoor jackets, pizza boxes and non-stick coatings.
101303.m: PFAS repel water and grease at the same time.

101304.q: Which fluoroplastic, known for non-stick pans, was discovered by chance by Roy Plunkett in 1938?
101304.e: In a gas cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene, Plunkett found a white powder that turned out to be a polymer. PTFE is very unreactive and heat-resistant.
101304.m: Polytetrafluoroethylene was discovered by chance in 1938 and coats non-stick pans.

101305.q: In which firefighting agent were PFAS used in large quantities for a long time, which now pollutes soil and groundwater in many places?
101305.e: Fluorine-containing foams form a film that is particularly good at putting out burning liquids such as kerosene. This is how a lot of PFAS got into the soil at airfields and training grounds.
101305.m: Fluorine-containing firefighting foam is an important source of PFAS in groundwater.

101306.q: Why are PFAS a problem for people and animals?
a: They build up in the body and are hardly excreted
They immediately break down into fluorine gas in the body
They are broken down into sugar in the stomach
101306.e: PFAS are hardly broken down and are excreted only very slowly. That is why some, such as PFOS, are banned or strongly restricted internationally.
101306.m: PFAS build up in living things.

101307.q: Which method is often used in waterworks to remove PFAS from drinking water?
101307.e: PFAS attach themselves to the large surface of activated carbon. Ion exchangers and reverse osmosis are also used, whereas boiling does not help.
101307.m: Activated carbon can filter PFAS out of drinking water.

101308.q: How many carbon atoms does perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) have?
101308.e: The word part “octan” stands for a chain of eight carbon atoms. Seven of them are perfluorinated, the eighth forms the carboxyl group.
101308.m: Perfluorooctanoic acid consists of a chain of eight carbon atoms.

101309.q: Which international agreement of 1987 governs the phase-out of CFCs?
101309.e: The Montreal Protocol commits countries to banning ozone-depleting substances step by step. It is considered one of the most successful environmental agreements.
101309.m: The 1987 Montreal Protocol brought about the worldwide phase-out of CFCs.

101310.q: Which three researchers received the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on the depletion of the ozone layer?
101310.e: In 1974 Molina and Rowland showed that CFCs release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere. Crutzen had previously described the role of nitrogen oxides in ozone depletion.
101310.m: Crutzen, Molina and Rowland explained how chemicals destroy the ozone layer.

101311.q: What splits the chlorine atoms off CFC molecules in the stratosphere?
101311.e: In the stratosphere, high-energy UV radiation hits the CFCs and splits the C-Cl bond. The free chlorine radicals then attack ozone.
101311.m: UV light releases chlorine radicals from CFCs in the stratosphere.

101312.q: Which reaction is the first step in the catalytic destruction of ozone by chlorine?
101312.e: A chlorine atom reacts with ozone to form chlorine monoxide and oxygen. ClO then reacts with an oxygen atom, which frees the chlorine atom again.
101312.m: In ozone destruction, a chlorine atom is freed again and again and so acts as a catalyst.

101313.q: Who developed CFCs as non-toxic refrigerants around 1930 and also brought leaded petrol onto the market?
101313.e: Thomas Midgley was looking for safe refrigerants for General Motors and found dichlorodifluoromethane. Both of his best-known inventions later turned out to be serious environmental problems.
101313.m: Thomas Midgley invented CFCs and leaded petrol.

101314.q: What is the molecular formula of the refrigerant R-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane)?
101314.e: The name says it all: a methane in which two H are replaced by Cl and two H by F. R-12 was one of the most widely used CFCs in fridges.
101314.m: Dichlorodifluoromethane carries two chlorine and two fluorine atoms on one carbon atom.

101315.q: Over which continent was the ozone hole first described in 1985?
101315.e: Researchers of the British Antarctic Survey led by Joseph Farman reported a sharp fall in ozone during the Antarctic spring in 1985. The cold and polar stratospheric clouds favour the depletion there.
101315.m: The ozone hole was discovered over Antarctica in 1985.

101316.q: Why were the hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) introduced as a replacement also restricted by the Kigali Amendment in 2016?
a: They destroy the ozone layer more than CFCs
101316.e: HFCs contain no chlorine and hardly harm the ozone layer. But many of them affect the climate thousands of times more strongly than CO₂.
101316.m: HFCs spare the ozone layer but heat up the climate strongly.

101317.q: According to common estimates, how many ozone molecules can a single chlorine atom in the stratosphere destroy before it is bound?
101317.e: Because the chlorine atom is released again and again in the reaction cycle, it acts as a catalyst. The chain only ends when it is bound in reservoir compounds such as HCl.
101317.m: One chlorine atom can destroy about a hundred thousand ozone molecules.

101318.q: What was the real name of the doctor who called himself Paracelsus?
101318.e: Paracelsus was called Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim. The nickname is often taken to mean “beyond Celsus”, after the Roman medical writer Celsus.
101318.m: Paracelsus's real name was Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.

101319.q: What new approach to medicine did Paracelsus champion?
a: He used chemically prepared remedies made from minerals and metals
He cured illnesses only with prayers
He rejected all medicine on principle
He treated all patients only with bloodletting
101319.e: Paracelsus saw illnesses as chemical processes and used minerals and metals specifically as remedies. This approach is called iatrochemistry.
101319.m: Paracelsus put chemistry to work for medicine.

101320.q: Which famous principle of toxicology goes back to Paracelsus?
101320.e: Paracelsus realised that almost any substance is harmful in too large an amount, and that a poison can even heal in a small amount. This saying is still a principle of toxicology today.
101320.m: Whether a substance is poisonous depends on the amount.

101321.q: In which Swiss city was Paracelsus briefly town physician and professor in 1527?
101321.e: Paracelsus taught in Basel and gave his lectures in German instead of Latin. After quarrels with the scholars, he soon had to leave the city again.
101321.m: In 1527 Paracelsus worked as town physician in Basel.

101322.q: About which occupational diseases did Paracelsus write one of the first works of occupational medicine?
101322.e: In “On the Miners' Sickness and Other Diseases of Miners”, Paracelsus described lung diseases caused by dust and metal fumes. He knew mining from his youth in Villach.
101322.m: Paracelsus was an early describer of miners' lung diseases.

101323.q: Which metal is Paracelsus said to have given the name that is used today?
101323.e: Paracelsus used the name “zincum”, possibly because of its jagged crystals. The name later became generally accepted.
101323.m: The name zinc goes back to Paracelsus.

101324.q: Which word for a small earth spirit became known through a work by Paracelsus?
101324.e: In his book on elemental spirits, Paracelsus assigned beings to each element. He called the earth spirits gnomes and the water spirits undines.
101324.m: The word gnome comes from the writings of Paracelsus.

101325.q: Which opium tincture is traditionally attributed to Paracelsus?
101325.e: Paracelsus described a powerful painkiller containing opium, which he called laudanum. Later the name came to be used for alcoholic opium tinctures.
101325.m: Paracelsus is said to have introduced the opium preparation laudanum into medicine.

101326.q: What did Leopold Ružička receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1939?
a: For work on polymethylenes and higher terpenes
101326.e: Ružička studied large ring compounds and terpenes, such as fragrances and natural substances. He shared the prize in 1939 with Adolf Butenandt.
101326.m: Leopold Ružička received the Nobel Prize in 1939 for his research on ring compounds and terpenes.

101327.q: Which present-day country did the ETH chemist Leopold Ružička come from?
101327.e: Ružička was born in 1887 in Vukovar, which then belonged to Austria-Hungary. He came to Zurich via Karlsruhe and became Swiss in 1917.
101327.m: Leopold Ružička came from present-day Croatia.

101328.q: How many carbon atoms does a triterpene built from six isoprene units contain?
101328.e: One isoprene unit has five carbon atoms. Six units give 6 · 5 = 30 carbon atoms.
101328.m: Terpenes are made of isoprene units with five carbon atoms each.

101329.q: What is the rule formulated by Ružička called, according to which terpenes are built from units of five carbon atoms?
101329.e: According to the biogenetic isoprene rule, terpenes form in living things by linking C₅ units. Ružička refined it in 1953.
101329.m: The isoprene rule explains how terpenes are built from five-carbon units.

101330.q: Which special feature did Ružička discover in musk fragrances?
a: They have very large carbon rings
They consist of short chains without a ring
101330.e: Muscone has a ring of 15 carbon atoms and civetone one of 17. Before this, such large rings were thought to be unstable.
101330.m: Ružička showed that musk fragrances have very large carbon rings.

101331.q: For which branch of industry was Ružička's research in Geneva particularly important?
101331.e: In the 1920s Ružička did research for a Geneva fragrance company that later became today's Firmenich. His work made artificial fragrances possible.
101331.m: Ružička's fragrance research shaped the Geneva perfume industry.

101332.q: What is Hermann Staudinger, Ružička's teacher, known for in chemistry?
a: He founded the chemistry of macromolecules
He developed the synthesis of ammonia
He drew up the periodic table
101332.e: Staudinger showed that plastics and many natural substances consist of huge chain molecules. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 1953.
101332.m: Hermann Staudinger is considered the father of polymer chemistry.

101333.q: At which university did the chemistry Nobel Prize winners Leopold Ružička and Vladimir Prelog do research?
101333.e: Ružička brought Prelog to ETH Zurich in 1941, where he later became his successor. Prelog received the Nobel Prize in 1975 for work on stereochemistry.
101333.m: Ružička and Prelog made ETH Zurich a centre of organic chemistry.

101334.q: Which processes in molecules does infrared radiation mainly excite in IR spectroscopy?
a: Electron transitions in the atomic nucleus
101334.e: Infrared light has the right energy to make bonds stretch and bend. Each vibration absorbs at a particular wavenumber.
101334.m: Infrared spectroscopy measures how bonds in molecules vibrate.

101335.q: In which range does the strong band of a C=O double bond typically appear in the IR spectrum?
101335.e: Carbonyl groups in ketones, aldehydes or carboxylic acids show a very intense band at around 1650 to 1750 cm⁻¹. It is one of the most striking bands in the IR spectrum.
101335.m: A strong band at around 1700 wavenumbers points to a carbonyl group.

101336.q: How does an alcohol O-H group with hydrogen bonding typically show up in the IR spectrum?
a: As a broad band at around 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹
As a sharp band at around 1000 cm⁻¹
As a weak band at around 2200 cm⁻¹
As a double band at around 1600 cm⁻¹
101336.e: Hydrogen bonds lead to many slightly different O-H bond strengths. This produces a broad, intense band above 3000 cm⁻¹.
101336.m: A broad band above 3200 wavenumbers reveals an OH group.

101337.q: What is the region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ called, whose complex pattern of bands is unique to each molecule?
101337.e: Here many vibrations of the whole molecular framework overlap. By comparing with reference spectra, a substance can be clearly identified.
101337.m: The fingerprint region below 1500 wavenumbers is unique to each molecule.

101338.q: Which wavelength corresponds to a wavenumber of 2000 cm⁻¹?
101338.e: The wavelength is the reciprocal of the wavenumber: 1 / 2000 cm⁻¹ = 0.0005 cm. That is 5 µm.
101338.m: The wavelength is the reciprocal of the wavenumber.

101339.q: Which astronomer discovered infrared radiation in 1800 using thermometers behind a prism?
101339.e: Herschel noticed that a thermometer beyond the red light warmed up even more. He had detected invisible heat radiation.
101339.m: William Herschel discovered infrared radiation in 1800.

101340.q: What is IR spectroscopy mainly used for in the chemistry lab?
